utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're just being handed, marked D57, the transcript of the interview. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to mention that you find in the interview a part shaded in grey, and these are the parts that were not played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We've got the entire interview in front of us. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, to begin with, let us start with the map that this witness commented on. I think it was not in private session, so I assume we don't have to go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This, I take it, is the map of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the map that this witness started his testimony with. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. For the record, it must be noted it's Exhibit 326, tab 11. The witness has a copy? Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue, I should just like to draw attention to the fact that, according to my accounts, the examination-in-chief lasted 24 hours. You told me I would have 20 hours. So would you please reconsider and establish whether my calculations are right. I may be wrong. It is quite possible that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me deal with that. You are wrong, in fact. It was 20 hours. I noted it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, is it true to say that this was no secret map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. A public document. It was all over the Krajina. It was like a leaflet; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a leaflet but what it is; a map with data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with data: A summary, information on the back of the map, even a summary in the English language should it have to be shown or distributed to foreigners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know for what purposes it was used. I obtained it in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was issued by the Serbian army of Krajina with the help of the journal Vojska from Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says, with the assistance of the publishing institution Vojska of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And there's the stamp of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and the stamp of the Serbian army of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The new emblem from 1994, or coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please comment, as you did before, with regard to this map, but first of all, before you do that, please tell me, what was the percentage share of the population in Knin municipality by ethnicity. In Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Knin municipality had about 90 per cent of the population were Serbs, or up to 90 per cent, and 10 per cent were others. Nine per cent were Croats, about 1 per cent were Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that would roughly be the composition in 1981.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may be wrong, plus or minus 1 or 2 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the leadership of the Republic of Srpska Krajina would frequently emphasise the fact that Croats in Knin were living on a footing of equality like all other citizens and that the authorities of the Republic of Srpska Krajina are not behaving towards the Croats in the way in which the Ustasha authorities are behaving towards the Serbs? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats know best how they lived in Knin, as do the people from Serbia and Knin. I will give you just three examples. There is no doubt that they didn't feel at ease during the time of inter-ethnic disagreements and conflicts, but it is also a fact that already in October some citizens of Croatian ethnicity and Albanians suffered damage because of the events in Knin. In April 1991, the police of Krajina selectively started seizing weapons from citizens - not all of them, but from Croats - and this especially happened in the village of Potkonj in Kninsko Polje, and Vrpolje. They experienced unpleasantness or worse than that, certain suffering. The inhabitants of the Croatian village of Kijevo, on the 26th of August, 1991, during the attack of the JNA. Also in 1993, Croats in Knin felt not only unsafe, but they were physically mistreated by refugees from Benkovac after the attack of the Croatian army on Ravni Kotari, especially people from Islam Grcki and the surroundings who would come to Knin. The police brought them there in an organised fashion and instigated them to move into Croatian houses so that the Croats had to flee and seek shelter in the centre in Vrpolje, and then the police organised their resettlement by buses via Zitnic towards the territory controlled by the Croatian government. That is as far as Knin is concerned. I don't want to be cynical, but the Croats in Knin fared better, in spite of what I just said, compared to how they fared in areas where there were armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I remember, for instance, that Milan Martic said with pride that Croats in Knin were living in conditions of complete equality, which we received with the greatest measure of approval, and another colleague of yours, a protected witness, not quite as protected as you but also protected, confirmed that in Knin, the Croats did indeed live on a footing of equality. Are you denying that now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just telling you how equal they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that they were not equal in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I know that they didn't feel comfortable and that I know many Croats in Knin who felt in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You held a very important position. I won't name it now in public session. If you found that there were such cases of mistreatment, why didn't you prevent it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities in Knin acted in several ways to calm the situation. First of all, the staff for the defence of Knin, for the barricades, was disbanded. It was formed in Golubic or, rather, to be more precise, it was formed on the 16th of August, 1991, in Padjeni, and it was based in Golubic. And then also, efforts were made to disband the Council of National Resistance which caused the greatest amount of confusion and disturbance when that was not necessary. And also, endeavours were made through the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina to place the police under the control of the government and civilian authorities, and a lawyer was appointed to the position of Minister of Internal Affairs in the government of SAO Krajina. Also, at the beginning of August, also through the government of Krajina, measures were undertaken for the police and the DB to be subordinated to the legal authorities of Krajina. This was also done on the 21st of November, 1991, through the Assembly of SAO Krajina. Such measures were also taken in February 1992, but by then, the position of the authorities that were behind these measures had weakened. This was not achieved because you supported those structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this witness, your colleague who spoke before you, said quite the opposite. Which structures? I hear for the first time this term of parallel structures. This is information that I received from you now, that you had parallel structures in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were structures formed by the DB of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, Frenki, and you personally. Those structures, in 1991, on the 16th of August, 1990, sought to obtain legitimacy by winning support of the Serbian Democratic Party, and they did get it at a meeting of the Main Board in Padjeni on the 16th of August, 1990. However, those structures started operating in a manner that was not originally thought necessary. The idea was for the Croatian government should not affect the position of the Serbs regarding autonomy. However, those structures that were formed in Golubic referred to the authority of the SDS and the authority of the president of the municipality, and they didn't form a staff to control the barricades but a war camp. And upon the initiative of the president of the Assembly, the Executive Board of the SDS, at the beginning of September 1990, decided that those structures be disbanded. And the president of the Assembly persisted in that direction, and that camp was disbanded. Martic was in charge of it in a wood at a first, then in a meadow, then at Cinobadova Glavica, the memorial home, then the Knin fortress. And from the 30th of September onwards, it moved to the police station in Knin. Jovica Stanisic, in August 1990, was already in contact with those structures. And those structures took over control over the Centre for Information of Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Let the witness finish. But can you keep your answers fairly short, M. Babic, so that the accused can have the opportunity to ask his questions. Is there anything more you want to add to what you were just saying about the structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This structure started to be formed in 1990. It was publicly announced over the Council for National Resistance, and later on, that structure operated in conjunction with the Secretariat for Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Interior of SAO Krajina as a parallel structure to the extent that they were not subordinated to the legal authorities of the SAO Krajina, though the authorities of Krajina did take part in the nomination of certain individuals in that structure for a particular purpose, such as was the case with Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's a Serbian saying which implies causing confusion. Now, tell me specifically, who were the people who constituted that parallel structure? Tell me the names of the people in that parallel structure in 1990 in Knin and the surroundings. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Martic, Jovo Vitas, Nebojsa Mandinic, Jovica Stanisic, the journalist Cvetkovic, an unknown individual whose name I don't remember from the room for encoding, and other people who were connected to them from the SDS and from among the citizenry. That was the structure that I identified in 1990, beginning with August through the autumn, until January 1991. In 1991, that structure consisted of Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic, Milan Martic, Dusan Orlovic - of course, Dusan Orlovic was there in 1990 as well - and people under their control and influence right through the presidents of the municipalities of Lapac, Korenica, Benkovac, the vice-president of the government, Dusko Starevic. And later, Veljko Matijasevic, the president of the Assembly, under the influence of Stanisic, joined in in 1992. Under your influence and that of Jovica Stanisic and Budimir Kosutic, Mile Paspalj joined in, and from the 16th to the 26th of February, that structure managed to assert its formal and legal authority in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. It's becoming clearer to me now. Do you consider all the officials in the Republic of Srpska Krajina and, before that, in SAO Krajina, who were in confrontation with you to constitute a parallel structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but those who did not respect the decisions of the government and Assembly of SAO Krajina and who used coercion upon members of the government to be tolerated, they prevented by force the government and the Assembly to assert their legal authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were they? Were they a faction in the SDS or were they members of other parties? What were they? What kind of a structure were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the DB of Serbia, members of the so-called DB in Krajina, members of the police of Krajina headed by Milan Martic, a part of the politicians in the SDS and outside it, and other people who were not in the SDS but who collaborated with the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean the DB of Serbia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cooperation, obedience, coordination. That's what I mean by collaboration. The DB of Serbia had no competence over the territory of Croatia in 1990. In formal terms, it could have no competence to govern or to run the police in SAO Krajina and the Republic of Krajina in 1990 and later, and it did that nevertheless. So its presence in the area was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the DB of Serbia was not competent in Krajina I quite agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In formal and legal terms, it was not competent, but it did have a command position over the structure, consisting of the people I have listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please don't get so excited. Without any excitement --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not getting excited. I'm trying to be as brief as possible in response to what Judge May has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, both of you, both of you bear in mind that this has to be interpreted, and bear in mind too what I said earlier, before the cross-examination began, about breaks between question and answer. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. May. I'll join in in what you said, because quite obviously this is highly interesting, not to say amusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you've enumerated Martic, Vitas, Orlovic, a man called Nebojsa whose surname you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mandinic Nebojsa, the president of the Assembly of Associated of Labour of the municipal Assembly of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Man -- what was the other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mandinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, Mandinic, the president of a Chamber of the municipality of Knin because the chamber had the Chamber of Associated Labour and the Citizens' Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, socio-political one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, socio-political.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Socio-political and the Chamber of Associated Labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the presidents of the three chambers. And what was Martic? Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a police inspector at the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time that the SAO Krajina was formed, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the SAO Krajina was formed, he was in the Council for National Resistance, and on the 4th of January, 1991, the Executive Council, Provisional Executive Council of SAO Krajina promoted David Rastovic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Knin and vice-president of the Executive Council of SAO Krajina and appointed him secretary of the interior for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You had nothing to do with that, no participation in that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the proposal and so on and so forth, as a man behind the looking glass, as you said yesterday. So Martic was Minister of the Interior for Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Secretary of the SUP, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs of Krajina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where is Martic from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martic was born in the village of Zagrovic, near Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Martic was secretary of the SUP of Krajina. He was from Knin. That first man. Now, who is Vitas? Who is this other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovo Vitas; he was a businessman in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A businessman in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he lived in Knin. Where he was born, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is he from Krajina, Jovo Vitas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where he was born exactly. The surname Vitas existed around Bosanska Krupa as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's not too important. But he was in Knin as well; is that what you're saying? And this man Orlovic, what was he? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Orlovic was a medical student. He never graduated. And he was a native of Lika. And he sort of did nothing much, went around without a job. But from 1989, we knew that he was always present when any of the events took place in the area, any important events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was his function, his post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was member of the Council of National Resistance. Martic appointed him as head of the DB, the state security in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the head of the state security in Krajina. And you say that he was originally from Krajina himself. That's right, isn't it? And were they members of any party, any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martic wasn't. Orlovic, as far as I know, wasn't either. Jovo Vitas, as far as I know -- I'm not quite sure whether he was a member of the Socialist Party of Croatia, of a Yugoslav orientation, but he did have some participation in preparations -- in the organisation. Then there was Nebojsa Mandinic, who was a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: This man Nebojsa, Nebojsa Mandinic, apart from the fact that he was president of this Council of Associated Labour, or whatever it was called, of the Municipal Assembly of Knin, did he hold any other post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Post, you're asking about, what post he held. Well, together with Bogoljub Popovic and Martic, he had something to do with some security matters. I can't really be specific what the name and title was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you were together there. They weren't there alone, the two of them on one side and you on the other side. I assume that all of you were together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each one of us in our own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understood it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The interpreters are having trouble hearing. Is your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem is not allowing pauses and not allowing the registrar time to switch it on, so can you bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So that means that we can -- we have to make pauses; is that it, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were saying Martic, the secretary of the SUP; Vitas was an official there; Orlovic was the head of the DB state security for Krajina; Mandinic was the president of one of the chambers of the municipality of Knin. How can they be parallel structures, then? How can a parallel structure be made up of people who hold official posts in the regular structure, even before the SAO Krajina was proclaimed? What kind of parallel structure were they, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What they were doing was not the structure of the institutions which were legally elected and established at multiparty elections. They were structures which had illegally cropped up, arbitrarily, on their own initiative, and that is why I call them parallel structures to the legal institutions. And I said that Martic was elected as secretary of SUP. But the Assembly of Krajina, following a proposal by the Prime Minister, appointed him Defence Minister for SAO Krajina on the 29th of May. And he himself, on that particular day, took the oath of office. And the very next day, having been convinced by Frenki and people from the DB of Serbia, he refused to hand over to the Ministry of the Interior, and to the newly appointed minister, to hand over his office to Dusan Vjestica. And in that way, it was through the force of might, because, together with the DB of Serbia, he had control over the armed formations of both the police force and the paramilitaries which had been set up in the camp of Golubic in April. So quite simply, he had might and power behind him, and the government and Assembly were not able to impose Vjestica, or rather, to force him to hand over his office to Vjestica. But one month elapsed, and on the 27th of June, in Grahovo, the Assembly was forced to accept his will in order to avoid an internal conflict in Krajina or a civil war at a point in time when the conflict was escalating with Croatia. So it was in that sense that he and they made up the parallel structure, once again in power in Krajina. They imposed their own will through force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, explain this to me, please: As you have just said - I hope I'm making sufficient pauses, Mr. May - that the Assembly lent its support to the positions of Milan Martic, how, then, did you say that he achieved his goals by force? Did he perhaps cock his rifles at the deputies in the National Assembly, or did he perhaps arrest a national deputy, or did anything else of that kind? So why are you fabricating nonsenses of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he did do that in 1995, and I complained to you personally that units of the police force had stormed the area. They had come in from Bihac and stormed the Municipal Assembly of Knin. I complained to you personally and asked you to intervene to quell the situation. And in 1991, he had the power because he was in control, together with the DB of Serbia, the state security system of Serbia. He controlled the regular police force and the police force of Krajina, the one that was established as the Krajina police, that is to say, the paramilitary formations that had already been formed. And after Dusan Vjestica took over power - or rather, he didn't take over power, I beg your pardon, but the Assembly nominated him and appointed him to the post of Minister of the Interior - he passed decisions to replace at least two deputies, two of Martic's deputies. And they, Martic and his assistants, tore up those decisions by the newly appointed minister and made fun of him and the decisions. So there was no other structure, nor was there any possibility of imposing -- of having Minister Vjestica take up his role. Now, to avoid an interior conflict, an interior clash and a civil war between the Serbs in Krajina, or amongst the Serbs in Krajina, this was accepted as a fact, that is to say, the authority of the DB and the authority of Martic, who was in command of the police force, because they had their own political goals, that is to say, the same political goals, which were that of defending a Krajina. So from that time, this parallel structure began to function; not only from that time, but it was functioning with those same political goals: to preserve Krajina within Yugoslavia, or rather, within the state that you yourself created. And the interests of the Assembly and government was also to preserve Krajina and defend it from attacks by the armed forces of the Croatian government, and that formed a symbiosis of a kind. However, this parallel structure - the paramilitary formations, the police of Krajina, the DB of Serbia, with its paramilitary units - did not only protect and defend the inhabitants of Krajina but caused provocations towards Croatian threats to create clashes and to pull in the Yugoslav People's Army, to pull it into the conflict, as you yourself had planned. And that is why the policy of these parallel structures differed from the political goals and endeavours made by the government and the Assembly, that is to say, the legal structures of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: Wasn't it your objective too to preserve Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was precisely saying that yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you something now. Did you say, on the first day in court here, that in 1990, what had happened there was that the head of the state security of Serbia turned up, Jovica Stanisic, along with his assistant, or whatever you called him, Franko Simatovic? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic came for the first time in August 1990, and at the beginning of April, Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic; Fica; your personal security detail or somebody from your security, Captain Dragan; another man who had a name that associated -- that brought to my mind France; and some other instructors turned up after their meeting with you, that is to say, after the second half of May, in order to -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: M. Babic, you should remember that -- try and keep your answers fairly short, because otherwise time is going to go on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see. The head of security of the DB, Jovica Stanisic, was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear the start of your question. The question wasn't interpreted into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1990. The head of the DB of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, was in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know his function in 1990. Martic said that it was a man from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, in 1991, you said again that with Radmilo Bogdanovic, this minister, this head of the DB, attended a meeting that was held at my office in March, and you mentioned something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radmilo Bogdanovic at that time was the outgoing minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And Stanisic was the head of the DB; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was the head of the DB, but from the month of April, he told me that he was the head of the DB, the state security. I heard this in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he told you that. So once again that is another lie. Jovica Stanisic was not head of the DB, either in 1990 or in 1991, when you're talking about this meeting. I didn't even know him in 1991. Nor could he have been there at that particular time on any assignment whatsoever. You could have said that I was in Croatia at the time, because I was holidaying in Dubrovnik, or rather, Kupari. And yes, I was. I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the head, and he talked to me about his personal conflict with Janackovic, and that was in March. He had these clashes with Janackovic, who was his boss. He had an office right next to Janackovic in the old building of the MUP of Serbia in Knez Milos Street, and he told me about his clashes with Janackovic. After that, Janackovic left, and he was the head. Whether his title was "head" or "chief" or whatever it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you say he had an office in the MUP building of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP of Serbia had a new building in Knez Milos Street, and his office where he received me was in the old building. Now, whether it was the MUP building, but it was an old building right next door to the new MUP building of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I heard in part of your testimony that he had an office in my office or, rather, in the building of the Serbian state Presidency, and now I hear he has an office in the MUP of Serbia, and this is quite a large evolution in comparison to your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September 1991, his seat was in his office next to Goran Milinovic, I think the man's name was, your man, your chef de cabinet, and he personally showed me, before I arrived at my meeting with you, the reporting room. It was a semi-oval room with a table in it. It had a stand for a map, and the room was empty. And that was in September 1991. And I met him in your office there in the autumn of 1991 and once more, I think. I said that he was in your office in March with Bogdanovic. I met him there once again in September 1994. I met him in your offices. You had invited him to come in April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When I ask you that, you can tell me your answers. Very well, Mr. Croatia-061.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And he had an office later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: M. Babic, let the accused finish his question and don't interrupt. He should not interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. He interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's put it that way. I interrupted you. That's just as exact as what you were saying beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't comment either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you were mentioning a moment ago that there was some parallel military units set up by them and led by them, and my question to you is the following: Are you aware, do you know that as far as Serbia is concerned - now I'm being quite specific here, Serbia - as far as Serbia is concerned, paramilitary units were only set up by opposition parties? Do you know that? Are you aware of that, Mr. C-061?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of the fact that Serbia or, rather, you, via Jovica Stanisic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and Franko Simatovic nicknamed Frenki, formed volunteer units, detachments, in the SAO Krajina starting with April 1991, and I know that you instructed and linked up the Secretariat of the Interior or, rather, the police stations on the territory of SAO Krajina, and also that you, through them, set up special units, the ones that the Assembly of Krajina, on the 29th of May, 1991, called the Krajina Milicija, militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the formation of your Krajina police force you considered to be the formation of a paramilitary formation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a paramilitary formation because it was not under the control of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can the police SAO Krajina not be under the control of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the way I explained. It had the right of might and was not subjected to a government that did not have sufficient might.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what about the Minister of the Interior? Was he at the head of that police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained how he came to be the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you explained that he was nominated and appointed by the Assembly. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In such a way that this was done by force, because he didn't wish to hand over his authority which the DB of Serbia and he himself had set up, the structure he had set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that Milan Martic was appointed by the Assembly of Krajina to the post of Minister of the Interior? Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he even took an oath of office, but he didn't want to. I apologise. He was appointed Minister of Defence, but he didn't want to hand over the Ministry of the Interior, and he took over this position by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly decided that he should hold both posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In formal and legal terms, the Assembly did grant him both posts because he demanded that and took it by force, and did he not hand over the other office to the Minister of Defence who was supposed to take charge of the special militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was any information ever published about this or was anybody informed of the fact that this decision by the Assembly of the Krajina on the appointment of Martic came about by force and that he did this by force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the people who took part in all this who know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are explaining your quarrels to us as if they are political events. What do I care about your quarrels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were not quarrels. This was the way you controlled and influenced events in the Krajina. You took over the armed forces in the Krajina through the DB and through Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I took over under power in the Krajina, what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fighting for the Krajina in -- by political means and taking part in those armed formations that were defending the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the paramilitary units. You say that what became the Krajina police was in fact a paramilitary formation. Do you know anything about paramilitary formations? Who set them up? Did the parties you cooperated with, and that was the entire opposition in Serbia, was it they who set up the paramilitary units in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I started cooperating with the opposition in Serbia in 1993. In 1991, up to March, we supported you and your policy, and we did this publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at page SA035981, which you handed over as an exhibit. When I say "you," I'm referring to the OTP. I don't know whether you personally gave it to them since you also belonged to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, that's a quite unnecessary comment. Can you identify, so that we can have it for the record, what this is and we'll find the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to read what it says here, as Ratko Mladic, the Commander of the Knin Corps, is sending his daily combat report to the commander of the 2nd Military District in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date of this document and the author?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 8th of April, 1992, and it says: "In the town of Knin and in the units, leaflets have turned up -" I'm reading slowing - "calling on citizens to attend the ceremonial launching of the brigade of the Serbian army in the village of Kosovo. Another brigade will be established in Lika, and the organisers forming these forces are," and then these are listed. And this was scheduled to take place at a certain time in 1992. And then it says: "The corps command, with the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence and the police of the Republika Srpska Krajina, have taken appropriate measures to suppress these intentions." So they have taken measures to thwart this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It's important that everybody else at a least has a copy of what you're reading from. Is this an exhibit? Can you help, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, as to what this is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not think that this is an exhibit, and we are trying to find the document with the help of the number given, but at the moment we are not yet successful. We don't know what it is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, was this one of the documents which were exhibited by the Prosecution or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, Mr. May. This is disclosure Rule 68, 31 October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. We'll try and track it down. M. Babic, can you follow what's being put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can assume what this refers to. If it refers to April 1992, I can assume what this is about. Is the date correct, April 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 8th of April, 1992. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Finish your question which I interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you comment on the fact that obviously the corps command and the Territorial Defence Staff and the police of the Krajina are taking appropriate steps to thwart these intentions of forming wildcat renegade brigade? And as you can see in this text, because I can't say your name, C-061, you yourself were the organiser of this. And Mladic responded, and the police responded in order to prevent this -- this running wild in the Krajina. Here it is. This was sent to the corps command and yet you are talking of paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Yes, you can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The question was put in the context of cooperation with the opposition in Serbia, but now I also see that it comes within the context of paramilitary structures. The events that took place in April 1992 on Dalmatinsko Kosovo near Knin was the formation of the so-called Serbian army when the Petar Mrkonjic unit was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Allow me one question about this. You organised this Petar Mrkonjic Brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If you mean personally, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean you personally organised it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you didn't. I will prove that you did. And secondly, is it correct that this brigade consisted entirely of criminals recruited by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please may I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, answer. You've already said that you weren't the organiser, so you needn't answer that, but you can give an explanation, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brigade was organised by part of the Regional Board of the SDS headed by Ljubica Solaja and Cubrilo. I personally attended that gathering and gave my support, for political reasons. In my estimation, this was a political demonstration and a protest against the demilitarisation of the Krajina. I can explain my personal and political reasons to the Court, if necessary, for doing this, but in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. You can just help us, though, as to what this brigade was. It's been alleged that it was a brigade of criminals. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a political protest against the demilitarisation of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness said that he could explain this but that he had to do so in closed session. I agree. Let us go into closed session for a minute, because I would really like to hear his explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to hear his explanation. 16 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following took place: In April, I was dismissed by the Assembly, the so-called Assembly, of the SAO Krajina after the appointment of the new government in Borovo Selo in February. In April, I was the President of the Assembly of the municipality of Knin and a member of the Regional Board of the Serbian Democratic Party. Part of this Regional Board, headed by Ljubica Solaja and Rade Cubrilo and some others, organised the so-called Serbian army. At the time it was a paramilitary formation as they envisaged it. I suggested that this would compromise us politically and that it would not be a good thing for us to do this. The people I talked to know this. Then they scheduled a rally on Kosovo Polje, and Veselin Djuretic, an historian from Belgrade, arrived. He was an advisor in the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. Mirko Jovic, the president of Srpska Narodna Obnova, with Kiro Radovic from Montenegro and some others arrived, and on that day, Veselin Djuretic, on the day he arrived, insisted that I should also attend the rally, and this was what prompted me to attend. I did so for political reasons, because this was the only political base I could rely on in the political confrontation with the structure that was then in power. I was then in the opposition, and that was the political reason I joined, in order not to be excluded. I attended the rally. I made a short speech supporting the event. I said before that to these people, "What will you do with this regiment once you've established it? Then you'll go home three hours later." And they had no answer to this. This was not a real regiment. It was simply a group of people. They wore folklore ornaments. Then they each went their own way after that. They brought the Petar Mrkonjic flag to my office in order to provoke me, and what did they do then? They asked the Executive Council to give them an office in the Municipal Assembly next to the office I had given to the UNPROFOR police. At that time, I was the president of the Knin municipality, and I had the UN flag flown, and I had given UNPROFOR an office in the Assembly building, and they made use of my weakness in order to get me to participate in a political provocation. Nothing came of it. It did not become a paramilitary troop. Later -- the later Minister of Defence of the -- or, rather, the Minister of Defence of that government in a place called Jelovi Tabani, or whatever it was called, in the valley of a little river flowing from Strmica among the hills in Lika, there was a warehouse there. So the Minister of Defence serviced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I think you may be drifting away from the point. Is there anything more you want to ask in private session, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says in this daily report by General Mladic to the command of the army: "The organiser of the formation of these forces is Milan Babic." That's what it says. And the corps command, the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence, and the police of the Krajina had taken measures in order to suppress these intentions. Therefore, you are the organiser of paramilitary units in the Krajina. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following is correct: Ratko Mladic was convinced that I was the organiser. Let me finish. Borivoje Djukic, a colonel who was subordinated to him and Martic, on the day that the rally on Kosovo took place, flew above it in a helicopter. Secondly, Martic said to me in Bijeljina, at a meeting organised by Karadzic with bishops of the Serbian Orthodox Church in February 1995 -- in February 1995, that is, there was a gathering in Bijeljina, convened by Radoslav Karadzic and the leadership of Republika Srpska, where the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church and a large number of bishops participated, and Ratko Mladic and I were invited. At lunch, Ratko Mladic asked me jokingly, "Where's your Serbian army?" I answered him and said, "You know better than I do." He looked at me in surprise. At that moment, it became clear to me that it was not Mladic but Jovica Stanisic who was behind the Serbian army in Krajina. That's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: God help me. Mr. C-061, you are engaging in science fiction now. But you said a sentence just a moment ago which I wrote down. This army was organised by the SDS of the Krajina and you supported it. So you simply supported it. But who was the leader of the SDS of Krajina? It was you personally, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was Ljubica Solaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Presidency of the Regional Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, SDS and the Serbian Democratic Party, that's the same thing. So it was your party, of which you were the leader, that organised this. You are simply trying to play this down by saying that you lent your support to it. But in Mladic's letter, it says that you were the organiser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this, we dismissed Ljubica Solaja. She did something else. And we dismissed her from the post of president of the Regional Board, and after that I became the head of the SDS Regional Board in Krajina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't replace Solaja because of this brigade and the paramilitary formations but because Milan Babic wanted to be president of that too; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan Babic wanted to keep in the political seat, as it is usually put in political lingo, and he did some stupid things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you did some stupid things because you wanted to keep your political seat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, figuratively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since we're in private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving from that document, do you want it exhibited, the Mladic document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. But you have that document. Yes, certainly I would like it to be tendered into evidence, please, admitted into evidence. It is your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the usher collect it and we'll exhibit it. What we'll do is this: We'll hand this to the Prosecution so they can identify the document. It should be translated. We'll exhibit it, and then this can go back to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll give it a number, first of all. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just to assist you: We do not have a translation of this document. This document was obviously disclosed as a Rule 68 submission. But we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you get us a clean copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we'll get it translated. The original can go back to the accused. We'll take the copy and have it translated. And give it a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked Defence Exhibit D58, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Are we finished in private session now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because I should like to take advantage of the opportunity and save time, because this is also indicative of the identity of the witness, so I have a few more questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You explained yesterday that your intention was, ever since 1990, to resolve everything within Croatia. And this brigade that you formed, you did so just like that, to provoke [as interpreted] yourself, because you just said you supported it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you, since there is a record in the transcript of what you said: You supported it, and it was organised by the Krajina SDS, of which you were a member of the leadership and later the president.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've been over these points, so there's no need to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And all this time, actually, you wished to resolve the problem within the framework of Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said my wish was -- in 1990 and 1995, that was my wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But tell me now, please: Did you, in your letter to me on the 11th of January - I have your letter here, with a stamp of your Republic of Serbian Krajina and your signature - did you write to me saying that my accusations against the Serbian people of the Republic of Srpska Krajina -- that my accusations were levelled against the people? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is what it says in the letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's your letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know the content, but I can't remember every single sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you write to me that the offered plan of Cyrus Vance implied the involvement of the peace forces throughout the territory of Serbian Krajina following disarmament? Did you write to me that this is being marked as a part of Croatian territory under UN protection and that those were the reasons why you couldn't accept it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that the constitutional legal system of Croatia would be implemented in those territories, and that such an adopted plan by me, while denied by you, was only one aspect of the plan that you adopted and that we objected to? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you have read is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you did all this with the wish, in your heart and in your mind, to resolve things within Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go on to another aspect, the duration. Do you remember well that I explained to you that we too had raised the issue in negotiations with Vance, but his response had been that the Security Council renews its decision every six months, on a regular basis, and that that would happen in this connection too, and we accepted this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an extremely honest man, open-minded in talks with us, and the Security Council did indeed renew the mandate every six months. No. After one year. Upon our request, the term of six months was changed to one year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that if the Vance Plan were to be accepted, there would be genocide against the Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fear of genocide did exist at the time, but not for the reasons that you had mentioned before the war, but because at the time we feared Croatian revenge for everything that had been done to them during the war in the autumn of 1991. We feared retaliation by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the plan that I accepted would not be accepted by the Serbian people of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I'm convinced that it is not acceptable for all non -- Serbs who are not indifferent to their history, and that that was your personal belief, which does not commit you. Do you remember that it was quite clear that the plan would not be implemented without your agreement, that is, the agreement of the authorities of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the proposal for the modification of the plan, we enjoyed the support of the people in Krajina. There was a large rally in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about that. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you were talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that the Cyrus Vance Plan was implemented only after the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had endorsed it? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You accepted the plan, and you forced the Assembly of Krajina to confirm what you had already accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have a specific manner of explaining facts. But did the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina - of course, following our maximum endeavours, and my own personally - did it accept the Vance Plan? Did I physically force the Assembly to accept the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You sent General Adzic, Kostic, and I was told that Glina was virtually blocked under military siege, more or less, and that also people who were not members of the Assembly were told to come to that meeting, and that that segment of the Assembly accepted it in that way because of the way in which you had brought it about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that what you're saying now about the blockage of Glina and people coming to the Assembly who were not members, that the military was widely present, you're saying exactly the same what some people from Kosovo said as to the way in which the amendments to the constitution of Serbia were adopted in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is a totally irrelevant point, totally irrelevant. It's not a question at all; it's just a comment. Now, what he said is that you forced them to accept it by sending generals and blockading. Now, you may challenge that, but that's his answer, so there's no point really going on about it. But while we're dealing with it, do you want that letter that you've referred to of the 11th of January, do you want that exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Tab 79.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we come to an exhibit like that - it's impossible for the Chamber to have them all in mind - can you let us know once you identify it? It will help us. Thank you. Yes. We've got two more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I write to you and caution you in my letter that between peace and war, every reasonable and honest man would choose peace, if the choice was between peace and war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says, but that was your trick. You publicly spoke about peace, but in fact you advocated war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I recognise this type of accusation, as you are not the best of pupils, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while, you were my teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but your present teacher doesn't seem to be so successful in teaching you the things you should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Come on, Mr. Milosevic. These are not proper questions. If you're going to make an allegation, make it clearly, but no point having an argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- I wrote that in the letter, and that is why I considered you an ordinary trickster, to put it mildly. Though you personally informed me that regarding the arrival of the UN forces, you would accept entirely the decision of the Presidency, you did the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not true that I ever said that I would fully accept the Vance Plan, and unconditionally. I always requested modifications, at all meetings: meetings with you, at General Kadijevic's, General Adzic, Jovic and Kostic, at the expanded session of the Presidency; and publicly, in the Assembly of SAO Krajina, the government of SAO Krajina, and addressing the people, I always advocated my views in public, and with great precision at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So just before the break, can we agree on one thing? On the tapes, when I listened to your beating about the bush regarding the plan, you just said that there was no discussions allowed, and now you're saying that you had discussions with Adzic, with Kadijevic, for three days, with the entire Presidency of the SFRY, at a session that you fled from, that you yourself said, when those discussions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were not discussions, Mr. Milosevic. That was coercion, to make me accept the plan unconditionally, without modifications, sir, former president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. Now, both of you must control your tempers. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will continue in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for the private session any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into open session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us clear up this business around Franko Simatovic, as you are accusing him of participating in the so-called parallel structure. Do you know what his position was in the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not accusing anyone. I'm just saying what I know. Secondly, I know that Franko Simatovic was subordinated to Jovica Stanisic and that you advocated, requested, demanded that he be in Krajina. You said that he was a good guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question. What was his position in the State Security Service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was subordinated to Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that he was head of the Intelligence Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion before the events in August 1991, you mentioned a man from the administration. I don't remember which number you used. You used a number, the second or third administration, and you said that there were certain criticisms about an individual as to why he was heading that service whereas he was a Croat by ethnicity. And then you said his father was a partisan and that he had chased the Ustashas and that he was a good guy. At the time, I didn't know who you were talking about. Later on, I learnt that you meant Franko Simatovic, who was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now you've added another fact. Do you consider that someone who is by ethnicity a Croat had ill-intentions towards the Croats, the Croatian people to which he himself belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you believe, since you yourself have said that he has said that he's a Croat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not a proper question, that. It's a pure comment. The witness can give evidence about facts as he knows them, and he's given the evidence about this man. That's purely a comment that you're making.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked: Do you know whether Franko Simatovic was head of the Intelligence Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what he was head of. I know he was subordinated to Jovica Stanisic and to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That he was subordinated to Jovica Stanisic goes without saying, as he worked in the state security service. And from the time that Stanisic became head of the state security, he was certainly subordinated to him. But I asked you whether you knew that he was head of the Intelligence Administration, which means that he collected intelligence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that from the DB of Serbia certain parallel structures had been formed, and you listed all people from Krajina, not from the DB of Serbia; Martic, Vitas, Orlovic, Nebojsa, Martinovic or whatever, and so on. And since you are claiming that the DB of Serbia was omnipresent there, tell me, throughout that five-year period, can you list people, ten names from the DB of Serbia who may have come to Krajina even for ten minutes throughout that five-year period? Can you give us those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just now I can remember Jovica Stanisic, Franko Simatovic, Fica, Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. What has Captain Dragan got to do with it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness finish what he's saying, then you can ask the questions. Now, are there any other names that you want to add, M. Babic, to those names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marko, I think, from later years. Just now I can't think of any other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you've listed four names of which Jovica Stanisic was based in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've said about Jovica Stanisic, who told me that Captain Dragan was in their service in August 1991, and he even mentioned some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He couldn't have told you that, because Captain Dragan was never in the state security service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please. I ask the Court to be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is preventing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic told me that in August 1991 in the Seher restaurant in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you say. You say he told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, his wife was there too, and she was born in the environs of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. That's great. You were at a private lunch with Jovica Stanisic and his wife.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He invited me to explain to me that Captain Dragan was a very strong-headed man and that they found it difficult to control him. Hot-headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could they have trouble in bringing to heel somebody who belonged to their own service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to divert attention from Frenki. I asked you to withdraw Frenki from this structure, and they wanted a public debate with Captain Dragan and people from the Krajina, as if this were a political conflict, to make it appear as if Captain Dragan was a political personage and not a member of the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know whether he was a political figure or not, but you do know that he wasn't a member of the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he was in the service of the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Neither was he in the service of the DB of Serbia, but let's leave that alone and let's move on. You were shown here a solution or, rather, a judgement by the court in Sibenik where an investigation was launched, and you stated your views about that. I think that was in open session. I think it was the judgement of the court in Sibenik that we were talking about. And the number of that document was 01397042.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you got the document. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said, as far as I was able to jot down --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to clarify whether it is the court in Split or Sibenik, and we would have to go into private session if that is the judgement referring to the leadership of the Republika -- the leadership of the RSK, because that was discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sibenik was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist the Court, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the arrest warrant for Milan Martic and the document that attends it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Exhibit 352, tab 111B, and it was discussed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was in open session, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, have you read the document in detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, if that is the document that I'm thinking of, there are two parts to the document. One part relates to crimes and the second to political crimes, if that is the document I'm thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness just have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decision made by the District Court in Sibenik, and the decision is to launch an investigation, and it is indeed in two parts in the explanations given. The first part relates to the person in question, and the second statement are reasons, and under number 1 it enumerates crimes, and under 2 it is for political crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a public session, an open session? Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this decision was discussed in open session. Do you recall that in your examination-in-chief you stated, when you were shown this decision, this decree, that the facts were correct? That's what you stated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under what is listed in point 1 and point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So let's look at point 1. It says the following, that from October to the present day, having formed an association of the so-called Council of People's Resistance... From October 1990 until today. So that is the Council of People's Resistance, or National Resistance. And you said that the facts contained therein were correct. Now, if the facts are indeed correct - and according to what you say, they are - then it is also true that the person under number 1 here, listed under number 1, was accused, and an investigation was launched against him. Is that correct, Mr. C-061?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said who the members of the Council of National Resistance were, and when questioned before this Tribunal, in my testimony, and over the past few days I spoke about the facts that I am aware of, stemming from this decision: the mining of the kiosk, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm asking you the following: You gave a very brief answer during the examination-in-chief. When you were shown and presented with these facts and this decision, you said that the facts were correct. Now, the fact stands here that the Council of People's Resistance, as it says here, and as you can see, you are considered responsible. Is that right or is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. 2 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned who the members of the People's Resistance Council were, and this was -- this decision was brought in by the district court in Sibenik and on the basis of the district prosecutor's office request. So these are the crimes that are listed: Under number 1, perpetrated by the members of the Council of People's Resistance; and then under number 2 there were other crimes which were political crimes, and I participated in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Can we take it, then, that under number 1 we have Babic Milan; number 2, Marko Dobrijevic; and then only in third place is Milan Martic, which was the reason you were asked this question; then we see that there is Nebojsa Mandinic; and number 5 is Dusan Orlovic. Right? So you are listed under number 1, in connection with what you state are the correct facts, that is to say, the formation of the Council of People's Resistance; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why, then, did you state that the facts were correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The facts are correct in the way that I explained them to be. These are suspects. It was the position of the prosecutor's office in Sibenik at that time. I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So the facts are correct, but only if they do not relate to you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I acknowledge this before this Tribunal: that on the 28th of February, 1991, the Serbian National Council, at a meeting presided by Milan Babic, brought in a resolution on separation of the Republic of Croatia municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika, of the so-called SAO Krajina, et cetera, et cetera. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't make a selection of the facts, which facts were correct and which were incorrect. You said that the facts were correct for the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point going over that. Just -- no point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No point going over that again. Now, M. Babic, you can tell us which facts you accept as being correct and which facts are not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the fact that all the crimes listed here are correct and that all the crimes do not relate to all the individuals equally who are listed here. Some of them relate to Milan Babic, others relate to Marko Dobrijevic, others yet again to Milan Martic, yet again others to Nebojsa Mandinic. So which facts relate to each of these individuals, I have already explained. I can go on and explain again if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you say that you -- it was your intention, although it wasn't on your lips, as you say, to integrate into Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were integrated into Croatia in 1990; and in 1995, it was our intention to go back, to go back to Croatia, to return in the status proposed by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that in due course. I didn't happen to notice among all these masses of exhibits here one particular order, which I have in my hands now, so I do apologise if I have omitted it. But here it is. I have it, the photocopy, in fact. It is the government of the SAO Krajina, the Ministry of Defence. The 26th of July, 1991 is the date. And it is an order pursuant to the constitutional law on the ministries and Article 32 of the Rules of Procedure of the government of the Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina. The Defence Ministry brings in the following order: that the Regional Staff of Territorial Defence for Kordun and Banija be set up, the headquarters shall be in Glina, and so on and so forth. Then he mentions the commanders appointed from Glina, who the assistants are, and so on and so forth. It comes into force immediately. And here it says: The Defence Minister, Milan Babic. And that is the 26th of July, 1991. Is that so or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
