utterances.text: You can take a look at this order if you like. Is it your own order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I please have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Here you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It sounds familiar, but I may be wrong about it. 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is correct in the original document, but this kind of order was signed by me, after a meeting with the president of the municipalities and the political leadership in Glina in July 1991, and after a political decision that was taken to abolish the 7th Banija Division and 6th Lika Division as ideological units which were not within the structure of SAO Krajina, and to proceed within the organisation of Territorial Defence of SAO Krajina as a legal structure of the armed forces for the Defence of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we have this admitted into evidence as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Subject to the Prosecution seeing it, we'll give it a number now and mark it for identification, and then if there's any objection, the Prosecution can make it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Defence Exhibit number is D59. It's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go back into open session, Mr. May, now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-061, what parallel structure are you talking about then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A structure which was not under the control of the government and the Assembly of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I see here that this is precisely, this document that I showed you, is precisely evidence of the opposite, proof of the opposite, that you had that control and not Jovica Stanisic or Franko Simatovic, that it was you yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a document that was in keeping with the provisions of SAO Krajina and its regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not challenging that. I'm saying that in keeping with the rules and regulations, you functioned to the full possible extent and not that the parallel structure was in operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was outside the line of parallel structure. This was along the lines of, first, a political decision to establish the Territorial Defence for SAO Krajina as an independent armed formation under the control of the organs of the SAO Krajina and one which would, in combat, function on the basis of the laws of Yugoslavia and the principles of a total national defence, or, rather, which would, should a war break out, be placed under the command of the competent structures within the JNA and the Yugoslav state Presidency during combat, in fighting. And it was be on the basis of the laws that would be applied as of the 1st of October. The political concept was that this structure should be the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exclusive control of the autonomous -- the autonomous control of the legal organs of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a point being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a technical point --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have just found that it is already in evidence, and it is Exhibit 352, tab 118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Remove the earlier number. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back for a moment to the map that you started off with and its background, because there are a lot of facts on it. I should just like you to comment briefly. Now, the introductory text that we received from you as to how the Republic of Srpska Krajina came into being, and according to this photocopy that I have here, it is on page 01132357. And it says here: "With the evermore aggressive Croatian chauvinism, the Serb people, in 1989, responded with the formation of the Serbian Cultural and Arts Society, named Zora, in Kistanje, and rallying ranks around national symbols and myths." Is that correct? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if the witness has got the passage first. Have you got it, M. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's correct that the Serbian Cultural Society --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer with yes or no, because there's no time for you to explain everything. I've read your quotation. Just tell me whether it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, because I don't know what the word "Croatian chauvinism" means here in this context. We used the word "Croatian nationalism" and "ethnocentrism." What the author wanted to say here, I don't know. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please comment on the following passage where it says: "The Croatian communist government, which together with the clerical nationalists sought for a way in which to trick the Serbs, responded with arrests." Is this correct? In 1989, you created the Serbian Cultural Society Zora in Kistanje, and the government responded with arrests. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrests came about not because the Zora Society was established but because of the incidents that occurred at the celebration of the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo near Knin when Zoran Jovan Opacic, the president of the Zora association, was arrested and a number other participants were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in June 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when your pictures first appeared in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then they say: "However, the nucleus around which the Serbian people will articulate their political platform was offered by the Serbian Democratic Party which was founded on the 17th of February, 1990, and Jovan Raskovic was elected its president." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says that: "This party was transformed into a movement of the Serbs, especially after the HDZ won the elections in Croatia in 1990, and their first step was the formation of paramilitary formations and illegal arming, and their platform was founded on secession and threats against the Serbian people." Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was the first or the second step, the one that refers to the establishment of the paramilitary formations and illegal arming by the Croatian government, but the police formations and the increase in the number of policemen carried out by the Croatian government was understood by the Serbs as being paramilitary formations, and it was so understood by the JNA as well. And there were associations of citizens belonging to the HDZ. And this was spoken of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the National Guard Corps? Was that the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was a police formation, but it was set up like an army. In other words, on organisational terms, it was a military formation but by its position it was part of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, tell me -- see what it says here: "Immediately after taking power, Franjo Tudjman and the clerical nationalists started introducing the symbols and signs of the Independent State of Croatia from World War II, opening up old wounds and inciting fear, often Ustasha genocide."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second sentence, "Franjo Tudjman and the clerical nationalists, immediately after taking over power, started with a party-of-right programme," this is exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the HDZ established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ was established in late 1989, and it was legalised a year later. Yes, in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you read the platform of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard what it was. I also listened to Franjo Tudjman speaking on Zagreb television during the pre-election campaign, explaining the party platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you read then in the party platform that there was a historical chance of establishing an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I listened to Franjo Tudjman on television saying that Croatia had an irregular geographical shape. It was boomerang shaped, and that it should be shaped by drawing a line along the River Drina. And he showed this on a map. So his conception was that Croatia should consist of the then-Republic of Croatia and the then-Socialist Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was the territory that used to be the Independent State of Croatia during World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know about history and the tales of people who were alive at the time, this was the territory covered by the Independent State of Croatia which also covered Srem, but the NDH did not cover a long part of the Primorje region which, when Yugoslavia was divided up by the fascist powers, belonged to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the second part. Tell me, then, is it correct that what it says here further on, the Serbian Assembly in Srb, on the 25th of July, 1990, issued a declaration on the autonomy of the Serbs in Croatia and a plebiscite of the Serbian people starting from the Avnoj decisions and the rights of nations and peoples to self-determination without denying this right to others. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says: "The attempt by the Croatian police to hinder the plebiscite by force, to stop it, and the events of the 17th of August, 1990, marked the beginning of the armed struggle of the Serbs for survival on their ethnic and historical territories." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're both being asked to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished. Could you please allow me to finish. On the 17th of August, the resistance to the attempts to prevent the referendum began, and later on during October 1991, this grew into -- into the causing of incidents by the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This referendum, what I read to you, was this initiated by someone from Serbia or was it a spontaneous reaction by you in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Serbia got involved in these events in such a way as to help the Serbs to organise a plebiscite. Serbia helped to define correctly the question that was to be put at the referendum in order for it to be within a legal framework. Serbia guaranteed with the JNA that the plebiscite, as we called it, or the vote, would actually be carried out. Serbia later got involved in these events in order to use them for its own purposes. This political conflict was used by Serbia, which got involved by setting up a parallel structure and causing incidents with a view to getting the JNA involved and the federal state to intervene in order to introduce a state of emergency and suspend the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are your assumptions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I be allowed to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are your assumptions as to what happened and what the responses were. Was the initiative -- did it come from Serbia or was it a logical reaction to the pressures and the repression to which the Serbs were exposed from the very beginning? Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said was not my assumption. These are facts for which I have personal knowledge and which I heard from the academician Mr. Raskovic. There are minutes from a session where he said that these clashes -- and he was speaking on the 10th of September in Srb in the evening, and he said there was a third party who wanted conflicts to break out in Croatia, that there were those in Yugoslavia who are bloodthirsty and who want to make use of the clash between the Serbs and the Croats in Croatia to introduce a state of emergency. These are facts, not my assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was he referring to, since you are putting forward these facts? Who in Yugoslavia was able to introduce a state of emergency in Croatia, and who was it who was bloodthirsty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Legally, it could be done by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, or it could be done by the JNA illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Raskovic criticise the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, literally, that it was a third party who wanted a conflict, not the Serbs and the Croats in Croatia. But I quote what he said: In Yugoslavia there are those who are bloodthirsty and who want to make use of this conflict to have a state of emergency introduced on that territory. And everybody knows who was able to introduce a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Raskovic criticised the army as being impotent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Raskovic criticised you, and in February 1992, he said that the army was weak. In February, after the Spegelj affair, when the army did not arrest Spegelj nor introduce a state of emergency in Croatia, he doubted that the army was able to do this. The army did this in a way later organised by you, starting on the 1st of March, 1991, and onwards; as far as I know, from April and May 1991 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was it that I organised from April and May 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You organised a parallel structure in the Krajina to cause incidents, and then you deployed the army on the confrontation line, in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We shall come to this later. Would you please comment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic mentioned the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- what is on the map, when the Croatian parliament, the 25th of December, 1990, in brackets, proclaimed Croatia the national state of the Croats and declared the Serbs to be a national minority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I brought this in order -- this map in order to show what the factual situation was and to show the participation of the JNA and the results of the war in the Krajina because of this. And I can comment on what the author here said; the cup runneth over and all of that, this is a literary way of expressing oneself. The rest is correct. In the constitution of 1990, Croatia excluded the Serbs as a constituent nation in the Republic of Croatia. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to the position of the Croats. You said that the government of the Krajina would never do to the Croats what the Ustasha government had done to the Serbs, and that the Croats were safe on the territory of the Krajina. And you even complained that the Croatian government was offering luxury hotels, Solaris near Sibenik, and Medena near Trogir, to accommodate citizens from those areas in order to get them away from the territory of the Krajina, and that this was a sly move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we're to follow these questions, we need to know what you're referring to, and I take it you're referring to the witness's evidence. If so, you should put the matter shortly to him so he can follow it. Have you followed this, M. Babic, what the accused has put to you? Start again, Mr. Milosevic. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-061, is it true that you all said to us in Belgrade that there was nothing for us to worry about because no one would touch a single Croat over there, that the Croats were equal in the Krajina, and that you had no intention of doing what the Ustasha government was doing to the Serbs outside of Krajina? Is that what you all said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you were asked to say how you intended to protect the Serbs, that is, to carry out your promise that they would be protected by the JNA. As far as I know, that's what the discussions with you were about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Witness, listen to the question. What is said is that you and others were saying they were not to worry, Croats were equal in the Krajina, there was no intention of doing what the Ustasha government was doing to the Serbs. Was that ever said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, things to that effect were said. What events exactly were referred to, I don't know, but if it would be put to me, I would comment on it, in early 1991. I have to say that the rhetoric, especially public rhetoric, escalated starting from 1990 and early 1991, after the Spegelj affair, after the outbreak of armed clashes, especially after the outbreak of war operations in the autumn of 1991. The mutual rhetoric, both Serbian and Croatian, escalated, so that in the 1990s, from the Serb side and the Serb Krajina side, the Croatian government and Tudjman and all their supporters were called Ustasha; and on the other hand, the Croatian authorities referred to the JNA as a Serbo-Chetnik army. So there was an escalation of rhetoric from 1990 to the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Do you remember that when we asked you questions, saying: If that is so - and we are glad to hear that you are making sure that nobody should be in jeopardy - why are Croatian families moving out of Krajina? And you answered: Tudjman is offering them luxury hotels: Solaris, near Sibenik, on the coast; Medena, near Trogir. These are large hotels. I personally visited them in the old days. And this is attractive to them, so they wish to give the impression that we are doing something against them, and that is not true. Is that true, that that was how you answered our questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session. 23 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember personally talking Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to Mr. Milosevic along those lines and about these matters. I did make a large number of public statements, different statements in different time periods, and I would like to know which period this is referring to so that I can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on, Mr. May? I see no reason for private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Can you help the witness? You're putting things to him, and in order that he can answer properly, he needs to know when it's alleged that these comments were made. When are you saying that he said all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have here any records of the meetings held, but this was a general issue, and it was a well-known position in Serbia that there must not be any discrimination along ethnic or religious lines, and that was the practice applied in Serbia anyway, and we expected the same practice to be applied by the leadership in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And I'm asking the witness whether it is true that they sought to persuade us that their practice was such that there was no reprisals against the Croats, that they were absolutely safe in those areas, and that they would not allow anything to be done to them such as the Croatian Ustasha authorities were doing to the Serbs. And I'm asking the witness whether that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In conversations with you, as far as I can remember, we mainly discussed the question of the protection of the Serbs, that is, the protection of the right of SAO Krajina to self-determination and remain in Yugoslavia. And you said the JNA would protect you, you have nothing to worry about. And therefore, my conversations with you were along those lines. Whether you discussed some other matters with someone else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you don't know, let me not insist on that. You are claiming that you don't know, though you all did say the same things in those days. Didn't your TO and the JNA protect you? Weren't you protected? And that this went on up until the Vance Plan, when the Blue Helmets were supposed to come and protect you, when there was no need for the JNA to protect you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a terrible, compromising protection, I can say as an introduction, but allow me to finish first. The JNA did protect the existence of SAO Krajina and the territory involved, but from August 1991, the JNA, together with all the formations under its command, covered the so-called referendum territory of SAO Krajina, went beyond it, and did some destruction and cleansing, forcing tens of thousands of Croats to flee. And it set up a border which was larger, beyond the so-called referendum borders, so that is the border that was shown on this map, the border taken up by the JNA, with all its formations, and over which you had command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the JNA did not establish any frontiers; it sought to position itself between the conflicting parties, not to allow Serbian and Croatian democrats to fight one another, the Democratic Community of Croats and the Democratic Serbian Party? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the police and the parallel structure, you instigated the JNA to go to that border, the confrontation line, between the months of May and August. And in August 1991, as far as I know, and everyone knows, the JNA launched offensive action. It went beyond that separation line and captured parts of Croatia which had not been Serb populated. It established a new line, a new border, virtually. That became the new border of SAO Krajina, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that easily, because that also is not true. Are they the borders that were protected areas by the UN? Are you talking about those borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This border doesn't fully coincide with the UN-protected areas. These areas are broader and larger than the UN-protected areas. They are larger by about 25 per cent. As for Western Slavonia, they are smaller than the UN-protected areas, roughly 20 per cent of the UN-protected areas in Western Slavonia; and in Eastern Slavonia, those borders coincide with the UN-protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about this map. I'm asking you about the facts, the factual situation as to where Serbs were living and where Croats were living, that factual situation. Those lines that you are referring to, were they the same that were later established as UN-protected areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the JNA lines, in the autumn of 1991, did not coincide with the ethnic territories of Serbs but went beyond, including territories where the majority population were Croats. Secondly, the zone or the line established by the JNA did not coincide with the UN-protected areas. Namely, the UN did not recognise parts of municipalities beyond those listed in the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's not waste time. Twenty-five per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we still in private session? Is there any reason why we shouldn't be in open session for this? Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see a single reason, Mr. May. You asked for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear that in 1991 the JNA was legally present within the territory of SFRY, regardless which territories in Croatia we're talking about, not only the territories that are on the map marked as territories of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, but in many cities throughout Croatia, where it had been for 50 years? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the question: whether the JNA was the legal army of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the territory of Croatia, not just Krajina. I'm talking about its legal presence throughout the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my God. The JNA was the armed forces of SFRY, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only it performed illegal acts as of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As to what is legal and illegal, let's leave that for later. But you say that in autumn 1991, you wanted to negotiate with the Croatian side, but no talks occurred because of your personal weaknesses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said -- you gave explanations that you wanted to talk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, with the Croatian side. Is that right? You spoke about that here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an opportunity through the international conference to establish a dialogue with Croatia and resolve the issue. That's what I did say. It was a good chance, but unfortunately, it was a missed opportunity, and I was one of those who made errors and omissions not to take advantage of that opportunity. It was a good opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could have answered simply with a yes without going into all those explanations. You said that you had proposed that Krajina should be a Zupanja in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990, during the discussions on the new constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that up to the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party in Glina and when you became one of the top leaders, you were an official of the League of Communists of Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the League of Communists of Croatia, and I held certain positions which I have already mentioned here in this Tribunal at the beginning of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer with a yes or no so that we can save time. You've already said yes with a rather lengthy, complex sentence. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In substance, no, because when you say "official," that means somebody with executive powers in the body of the League of Communists, starting from the Municipal Committee through the Regional Committees, the Central Committee, et cetera, et cetera. So when you say an official, you mean someone with executive powers in the structure of the League of Communists. So my answer is no, or exactly what I said in answering your question for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you claiming then that you were not in the Presidency of the Municipal Committee of Glina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you an official of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and, as such, a delegate at the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with this in private session. 15 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you, M. Babic, tell us what position you had, if any, in the League of Communists and whether you attended this congress or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1989, I was a member of the basic organisation of the League of Communists for primary health care in the medical centre in Knin. At the elections for delegates, for, I think it was the 11th and last congress of the League of Communists of Croatia at the elections organised throughout the structure of the League of Communists in Knin - it had 3.000 members - I was elected one of six delegates from the territory of Knin municipality to be a delegate at the congress that was being held in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why you need such a lengthy explanation. I am simply asking you whether you were a delegate at the congress of the League of Communists of Croatia and now you're saying yes, explaining that you were one of six delegates from the whole region elected to the congress. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because you started your question by saying whether I was an official, and I'm saying what that means. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not going to get into -- we're not getting into an argument about this. Now, do you want to ask anything more, Mr. Milosevic, about the League of Communists or anything of that sort? If not, we'll go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were a participant at the congress, and the congress debated important political issues. The League of Communists of Croatia was in power; you were participating at the congress of the party in power. Did you say anything at all in connection with those documents and decisions? Did you oppose anything that you disagreed with at that congress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember three things. First, at a commission for the reform of the economic system, I made a written contribution for the discussion, suggesting a reorganisation of the communities of interest in the social services and the formation of funds. Secondly, at a plenary session, when there were decisions regarding the statute of the League of Communists of Croatia, I was against the option which reorganised the League of Communists of Croatia in such a way that it should, as an independent organisation, join the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, because according to statute up to then, the League of Communists of Croatia was a part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. And a third point I wanted to oppose were writings by Mitrovic or whatever his name was, secretary of the League of Communists of Croatia, who gave an interview to Nova Makedonija newspaper and who spoke badly about Knin as a focus of nationalism. So this was on the bulletin board of the congress, and I wanted to debate this. But the delegation from Knin said, "Don't. Boro Mikelic will attack them and criticise them." And indeed at the plenary session Mikelic delivered a political speech. I don't remember all the details, but he spoke about it. So that was what I did at the last congress of the League of Communists of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Is it true that from a communist -- you were a communist, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists and a communist, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So suddenly, from a communist, that year, within a period of one month, you did an about-turn, a salto mortale, and turned into a nationalist. You completely changed your convictions, and from a communist you became an anti-communist and took over the leadership of Knin municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under your influence, I certainly became an ethnoegotist, and if I had listened to you until the end, I would have become even worse. As for the position of president of the municipality, I became that because I joined the Serbian Democratic Party on the 11th of February, 1990, in Knin, or, rather, I was invited to address the founding Assembly. And after my address, the people liked it, and they proposed me to the Main Board, and that is how I became a member of the Main Board. And as I had a lot of merit for the election campaign in Knin municipality, there was a discussion as to whether I should be a delegate in the Sabor of the Republic of Croatia or whether I should be president of the municipality. And it was my personal wish - I wasn't a good speaker in those days to go to the Sabor or Assembly - I preferred to stay locally in Knin, and this was supported by people from SDS in Knin and Jovan Raskovic, and the Executive Board decided to nominate me as a candidate for president of the municipality, and I did. I was elected as the SDS had a majority in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all this went along those lines because they were enthusiastic about you. They elected you. They didn't even ask you of your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes they did, to make the choice whether I wanted to be a delegate in the Assembly of Croatia or the president of the municipality in Knin. And for the reason I have given, I said that I wasn't a good speaker then and I didn't think I would fare well in the debates in the Sabor, so I said I would prefer to stay in Knin, and also because I had merits for the election campaign. I was very active during that campaign Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Knin municipality, part of Lapac and part of Benkovac, and wherever I headed the campaign, the party won the elect. So this was a reward for my political activities, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Kordun and Eastern Slavonia? The Serbs mostly voted for the League of Communists of Croatia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the elections in 1990, five delegates were elected to the Sabor of Croatia of the SDS of Serb ethnicity, and 27 delegates, members of the Serb ethnicity and members of other parties, and especially of the League of Communists of Croatia. That is the Party of Democratic Change as it came to be called. As for the municipalities, the SDS won in four municipalities. Actually, in those days, the SDS wasn't really ready, didn't have the necessary organisational structure to take part in the elections throughout the territory of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. It was weaker organisationally. So because of the way in which the president of the party led it in a leadership manner rather as a movement than a party, and because of its poor organisational structure, those were the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. All that was in Knin. Did anyone from Serbia exert any influence over you in that respect, in the change of your political orientation and everything that you've just spoken of, the events in Knin, the establishment of the Serbian Democratic Party, the taking up of the party course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say indirectly in two ways. First of all, Serbia advocated the federalist concept of Yugoslavia, which I accepted. And secondly, Serbia, through the media, starting in 1989, laid great emphasis - too much emphasis, I must say - on the position of the Serbian people in Croatia, and I believed this. I was even elected to the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party because I referred to the position of the Serbian people in the area between Knin and Karlovac in the way spoken of by the Serbian press. When passing through the area, I looked to see whether this was so. I saw dilapidated and ruined churches which had not been repaired. In Plitvice, I saw that Serbs were moving out of the area. There was a certain amount of depopulation, and that's what I said. I said that the communist authorities, that is the communists of Croatia or the Croatian communities, as I began to call Raca, had caused a desert to exist between Knin and Karlovac. That was my impression, and that was what Duga of Belgrade and Novi Sad television said. You asked about influences from Belgrade. Well, truly because of that impression and because of what they said, that's how I began to view things, and this contributed to my being elected to the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're now speaking of a tabloid in Belgrade that wrote about this. Did the official papers write anything at all about the position of the Serbs in Croatia in 1989? In Serbia, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Television Belgrade and the Novi Sad television, they broadcast a report on the population moving out of Plitvice. And there was even a writer from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the Belgrade media and the official press.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1990, there was a headline in Politika I remember about the failure to bury the victims of the Ustasha genocide from World War II and that this amounted to a repetition of the genocide. That's what Politika said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll find what Politika said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As regards the press, we will have time to go into this. Do you remember that in the speeches you made then you attacked both the communists of Croatia and the communist regime, as you called it, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that depends. There was a structure in the SDS which didn't criticise the communist regime in Serbia at all but criticised the communist regime in Croatia. The president of the party, Mr. Raskovic, the academician, after he decided to go to Belgrade and organise the party there, he said, "We have to make a decision ." At the famous eighth session of the Central Committee of Serbia when you carried out -- well, I'm not qualified to give an opinion about this, but some sort of party putsch, he said that one communist group had replaced another. And it was from that point onwards that he began to suffer criticism and mistrust from your side. There was a group in the SDS which supported you in spite of the fact that they sometimes overemphasised their national or one would say nationalist positions. And there was another group. Well, it wasn't really a group. It was Raskovic and Mihajlo Markovic, who was an academician, a member of the Executive Board, an ideologue of the SBS, and who said the following to me, speaking about Jovan Raskovic, the president of the SDS. He said: "We agree with him about one thing, and tomorrow he says another, and vice versa. And then Milosevic criticises him one day and praises him the next. We don't know what to do with him." And in the end, you withdrew him. You brought him back to Belgrade. You separated him from the people, and you started a campaign. Starting in July or early August, you started to weaken Jovan Raskovic for these reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who withdrew Raskovic to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dobrica Cosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you said at the end you withdrew him to Belgrade, but I met Jovan Raskovic only once in my life.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dobrica Cosic did it, but you, through your media, started a campaign against Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think there is no point in us being in private session, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started explaining something to do with the president of the SDS, Jovan Raskovic, which is incorrect, and therefore, I want to ask you the following. I think I can do this in open session. I won't mention your name. Is it correct that you held it against Jovan Raskovic that he went to Zagreb and had talks with Franjo Tudjman and other leaders in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two members in the Main Board. Both were vice-presidents of the party. One was the president of the Executive Board. And they laid great emphasis on such things. There was also a discussion at the Main Board of the party. Jovan Opacic, Zelenbaba, Branko Peric, and several other people asked that Jovan Raskovic be replaced, but they did not gain the support of the majority at that session of the Main Board. Jovan Raskovic was not dismissed. These people left the SDS after that session and went to the Serbian Renewal Movement of Draskovic. They said that the SDS was the Serbian infantry, that it was weak and inefficient and that they were crossing over to the artillery, to the SBO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that things were somewhat different from this. You criticised Jovan Raskovic strongly because of some compromising statements he made in his talks with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You probably mean other talks he had later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to your attacks on Jovan Raskovic. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What attacks? By me or by people from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you mean me personally, we can discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was you, together with someone I will not mention here by name because I would then be in danger of revealing your identity, on his return from America, you not only dismissed him but almost hounded him out of the Krajina, out of the SDS, out of all public life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Jovan Raskovic did not live in the Krajina. He lived in Sibenik. Secondly, Dobrica Cosic suggested that he go to Belgrade for certain reasons. And thirdly, the HDZ in Sibenik organised the signing of a petition against Raskovic, Marko Dobrijevic and Branko Popovic. And fourthly, from late 1990, a so-called Krajina faction of the SDS began to emerge within the SDS. Jovan Raskovic was never dismissed. He died as the president of the SDS in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that it is because of their disagreement with you in the way that Jovan Raskovic was treated that these people, Opacic and Zelenbaba, the people you mentioned who were co-founders of your party, left the party and went over to the SBO? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment they were leaving the SDS, I was very close with President Raskovic. They were one faction, and then later on, a harder faction, a pro-Milosevic faction which supported you was established consisting of Marko Dobrijevic and Petar Stikavac who were its leaders, and that's why Jovan Raskovic dismissed them in February 1991. After that, a faction was set up consisting of the Regional Board of the Krajina SDS and President Raskovic said that this was a faction which was not eliminated but tolerated because we were a democratic party. And several political options were allowed. President Raskovic said that anyone who uses his own head thinks a little differently from the next person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that you mentioned here that I had something against Raskovic, but now you explained that he left for quite different reasons and under quite different circumstances. And now you're saying that there were some SDS members who supported me at the elections. But why did I need their support in Knin when I was running at the elections in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two things: Firstly, in February 1991, you said that Jovan Raskovic should be dismissed. I told you personally he could not be dismissed; he was a popular leader. Secondly, you were waging an election campaign in Serbia in 1991 for the parliament, as the Socialist Party of Serbia, and you yourself were running for president. You had a conflict with the national opposition, and it certainly suited you to have the support of a party defining itself as a democratic and a Serbian party. This suited you politically, in order to gain support among the voters in Serbia, you and your party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: C-061, you said just a moment ago that in 1990 the reach of this party went only as far as Knin and maybe several kilometres beyond Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early 1990, in the elections up to -- leading up to May, but after that, the party founded its first committee in Belgrade and another in Novi Sad. And just before the elections in Serbia, the independent SDS of Serbia was established, which took part in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your party was in the opposition at the elections in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of the party split away and established an independent SDS of Serbia, taking part in the elections in Serbia, and part of the people and the Main Board of the central SDS party in Knin supported you, and that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. They supported me probably in their thoughts, because, as you know, we won those elections by a landslide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The support was in the media. I don't know what media transmitted this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you are denying that you drove Raskovic out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was your campaign, your underhand campaign, to disqualify him politically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This argument is of no assistance to us, in which you both interrupt each other. It's impossible to follow. Now, we're going to adjourn again for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll sit now until 2.00, and I understand the Prosecution may want a few moments at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To continue: It follows that Raskovic was not handed from Knin in your struggles for political prestige but for other reasons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain, then, whether you launched a campaign in 1995 to replace the then Prime Minister, Borislav Mikelic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1995, or rather, in 1994, with the replacement of Mikelic -- actually, this was initiated by the president, the then president of Srpska Krajina, and he was replaced in 1995, in June, I think it was. Mikelic was the Prime Minister, and he had a minority in the Assembly of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the dates. I have the dates here. What I asked you was whether you were at the head of the campaign to have Mikelic replaced, you and your party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If by that you mean whether there was a political decision to that effect, to have Borislav Mikelic replaced before there was a vote in the Assembly, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That wasn't the question. The question was: Were you at the head of a campaign? Now, it is a fairly straightforward question, M. Babic, so perhaps you could just answer it simply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can, if you tell me what is meant by "campaign." What does the word "campaign" imply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. It's a perfectly clear word, what "campaign" means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, just a moment in open session before we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Microphone for the accused, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you want us to go into private session, I'd like to ask one more question in open session, before we go to private session, so that we can clarify some circumstances with regard to the answer I'm going to get to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What I want you to explain is this, the circumstances surrounding -- or rather, the circumstances and the reasons for which you fled from Knin for three days, prior to the Croatian offensive, together with your wife, your children, and your mother-in-law. Why did you flee to Belgrade? Is that correct or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session now. 14 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know what I meant by the word "campaign."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in a private session now, as I take it, Mr. May. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So my question was: Did you wage a campaign to have Borislav Mikelic replaced, you and your party, the Serbian Democratic Party, whose president you yourself were, and, at the same time, the minister in that government of Borislav Mikelic, Minister for Foreign Affairs? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't want to call that a campaign. A campaign implies something broader, which involves longer political debates, et cetera. This was a political decision that was taken, and it was my initiative as well, and the initiatives of the deputies of my party, who won the majority in the Assembly of the RSK. And the decision was to initiate - and it did do so - and the decision was made to have Borislav Mikelic replaced as Prime Minister of the RSK government. So it wasn't a campaign of any kind; it was just a political debate, followed by political decision. The Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina, whose president I was, had the majority of deputies in the Assembly, but not the vast -- they weren't qualified as a majority. Borislav Mikelic had the minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the government of Borislav Mikelic, and Borislav Mikelic himself, along with my support, did he hold negotiations with representatives of the Croatian government to discuss a series of issues in which intermediaries participated, Owen and Stoltenberg, to discuss the normalisation of relations and all other outstanding issues that we'll get to in due course? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not precise enough to say "your support." It was your direct participation, in very concrete, specific terms. Those talks were not able to begin without your decision. A negotiation, an agreement, could not have been reached unless you agreed to it, unless you agreed to the text of the agreement itself. So an agreement could have been approved only once you had okayed it. And once I made a statement, a public statement, with respect to the agreement that I took part in, I made a further statement than you asked for. And then a whole edition of a daily paper called the Vecernje Novosti, for the provinces, you threw into the wastepaper basket because my statement went beyond what you yourself agreed to. So I said yes, your participation; yes, your decision to have the negotiations go forward; and yes for an agreement to be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, is it correct that the so-called Zagreb agreement was reached, and that your delegation was led by Mikelic, and that there were three points in the Zagreb agreement: The first was cessation to all hostilities, second was normalisation of economic relations, and third a political settlement to be discussed? Is it true that that Zagreb agreement contained those three points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is true is the following: A truce -- an agreement about a truce was adopted in March, before Mikelic and the government of Serbian Krajina were constituted, after the elections that were held at the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994. And next, the beginning of negotiations to discuss economic issues was after you had approved it in June 1995 and after direct talks were held between, on the one hand, Mikelic and myself, as Foreign Minister, and on the other side there were the deputies of the Croatian government, Sarinic and Ivica Pasalic. And that's how the negotiations began. The agreement was reached, that is, at the end of 1994. I don't know whether I made a slip of the tongue. It was 1994. And we spoke about the oil company in 1995, and you proposed a name for that mixed oil company. And those negotiations were completed, and the crowning glory of that was the agreement signed by Mikelic and verified by Sarinic and the government of the Republic of the RSK. I don't know which other Zagreb agreements you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Might you have made a mistake? Was it not in -- when you said in June 1994, that the negotiations were held in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said I misspoke. I might have made a slip of the tongue to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true, Mr. C-061, that you set up obstacles constantly to those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct. I took part in them to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that later on, when you took part and when you did not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The economic agreement and the talks pertaining to that point, I took an active part in that, and the agreement could not have been adopted in the Krajina Assembly without my political support and the support of the deputies whose representative I was, the party I represented, the party whose president I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what we're talking about. You controlled the extent and measure to which something would go through and would not go through. And isn't it true that Mikelic reached an agreement to open the motorway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mikelic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't seem to remember you being there, and I don't think Owen and Stoltenberg remember you either on the negotiations for the motorway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, isn't it true that for the most part you criticised Mikelic, and you said he wished to integrate Krajina into Croatia in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were two approaches towards Mikelic. The year was 1994, and then there was 1995, and different reasons and different causes and different reactions. So as far as Mikelic is concerned in 1994, it was through my initiative that his replacement was thwarted or, rather, I prevented this. I gave the initiative not to give a vote of no confidence to Mikelic in 1994 precisely when the economic negotiations started, and precisely so that the negotiations could be continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in 1995, when the negotiations started to bear fruit and bore results, then you considered that he was in fact working against the interests of Krajina to reintegrate Krajina into Croatia and then launched a campaign to have him replaced; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1995, this is what happened: The agreement was blocked, the implementation of the agreement was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, 1995. There was a blockade of the agreement with respect to the crisis and the new mandate for the peacekeepers, the UN peace forces. Mikelic was replaced after a meeting of the Assembly of the RSK, and this took place in May 1995. So at the following Assembly in June. The public reason given was that he was against the unification of the RSK and Republika Srpska. This was a way to gain support for his replacement with the minority in the Assembly. Now, the causes, the real causes lay in quite a different field. The reasons were that Mikelic, at that time, no longer came to Knin. He was afraid to cross the border, cross Republika Srpska into Knin. He would convene government meetings in Erdut, in Eastern Slavonia. And to all intents and purposes, he had contributed to the fact that the RSK, at that particular time, was divided. It was divided into the territory of the former SAO Krajina and Eastern Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go too far afield. Answer my question. Please stick to my questions, please. You now said that Mikelic was replaced in May 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that on the 30th of May, 1995, you were given the mandate by the president of the republic, Milan Martic, to form a government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mikelic was replaced in May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June. Or the end of May. Possibly the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the 30th of May, 1995, as being the correct date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was given the mandate to set up a new government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. So on the 30th of May, you received the mandate to set up a new government, and then you brought the whole structure, power, and authority into a situation of crisis, because it was only on the 27th of July that you in fact formed a government at the meeting in Topusko; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you contributed to that. The reason was obstruction. The police which you controlled in Eastern Slavonia did not permit the Assembly to take place in Mirkovac -- Mirkovci, for the government to be formed, established earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for two months you were not able to set up a government because you wished to hold the Assembly in the place where Mikelic had held his government and which you criticised him for keeping a government in Eastern Slavonia. Why didn't you have the Assembly in Knin, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We wanted to gain the political support of Eastern Slavonia, because the problem was Eastern Slavonia, in fact, because you had divided Krajina into two parts. It was your plan and Karadzic's plan that the former SAO Krajina should be liquidated and to have Eastern Slavonia remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that's not true. Neither Karadzic nor myself had any plans of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear about the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Buha, the Foreign Minister, Aleksa Buha, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Republika Srpska, and Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Buha and Krajisnik tell you it was my plan to divide up Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As they cooperated with Jovica Stanisic - Jovica Stanisic was your executor at that time - and on the basis of what you told me in 1991, this was a certainty for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was it that I told you in 1991 which presented a certainty to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That you would leave Tudjman with Bihac and the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by doing so that you would cede to him the territory of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true at all. You explained to us here in this courtroom that after the talks I had with Tudjman, I asked you, in order to release the tension that had built up, to open a road, a line of communication so that they could communicate with the Drnis area down there, and your reactions were that this was tantamount to treachery if they were allowed to communicate, that this was a betrayal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said that Tudjman needed Bihac. You said that loud and clear, and I understood that to be your agreement with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't have understood the agreement. You couldn't have understood anything, because a country needs roads in order to communicate. I don't have to explain that fact to anybody. But you held the government in crisis for two months, since you received the mandate to set up a government and until you actually did so, just because you weren't able to hold your Assembly meeting in Mirkovci, although I don't know why you couldn't have a meeting anyway on the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the events of 1995. March 19 -- in March 1991, you reached an agreement with Tudjman about Krajina. Those were my conclusions or, rather, you said so. That's what you said. And in 1994, on the 20th of November, this was confirmed by Aleksa Buha. He bore that out. And in January 1995, well, that was your concept. You controlled Karadzic through Jovica Stanisic at that time, although you came out publicly in favour of having it appear as if there was a blockade between Yugoslavia or, rather, Serbia and the Republika Srpska. You in fact controlled Ratko Mladic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Stop right there. Stop right there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you politicians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not just some sort of argument. Remember you're both in court. Now are we still in private session? Right. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you can ask a question. Keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please refrain your answers to answering my questions, please. You mentioned a meeting a moment ago that you came to see me with Martic, and at that meeting, you said you had heard me criticise Martic for lending support to Karadzic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the third meeting that you had with Martic, and I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So I was criticising Martic for lending support to Karadzic. And now you're saying, now you're saying that that conflict and the blockade itself was in fact rigged, whereas there was no kind of conflict and clash or blockade at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said what I quoted. You said to Martic that you weren't going to make a new Karadzic out of him, which means that you didn't want him to make political outbursts. That's how I understood it at that point in time. Of course, the public was informed that the government of Serbia or, rather, you yourself had introduced a blockade of Republika Srpska, but from what I knew, that blockade, as far as weapons were concerned and as far as fuel was concerned for army purposes and as far as wielding influence on Ratko Mladic and as far as Jovica Stanisic's activities were concerned in Republika Srpska, it did not in fact exist. There was no blockade of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that from Jovica Stanisic, Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik. I know it also from Borislav Nikolic. And in fact, the basic reason for which Borislav Nikolic was not able to cross over Republika Srpska territory was that he was in a conflict with Karadzic with respect to the fuel, oil quotas for Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to oil and petroleum later on, but tell me this: Is it true, at least what you said here, that it was in July of 1993 that you met and decided to set up a Serbian Democratic Party of Serb Lands which would go to the elections, go to the polls in Serbia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that there was an initiative by Radovan Karadzic at the time and of the Serbian Democratic Party of Serbia for a Serbian Democratic Party of Serbian Lands to be formed as a party, and I took part in those discussions, but those discussions did not end in the way envisioned by Karadzic, that is, the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina of which I was a president did not join that unified Democratic Party of Serbian Lands, because I insisted that the situation was such as it was, that there was separate republics. For as long as the RSK existed, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbian Democratic Party should be an independent party in that republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just list the facts, because when facts are mentioned outside of time and space, they give a different impression. I hope you will agree with me in that respect. Is it true that in 1993, in July, when you discussed the formation of a Serbian Democratic Party of Serbian Lands that in mid-May in Pale there was an Assembly meeting that I attended, with me the Greek Prime Minister Mitzotakis, the President of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic, when we insisted that the Vance-Owen Plan be accepted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they rejected that plan quite unreasonably and, after that, the blockade was introduced? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was published that a blockade was enforced by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that international observers came, an International Monitoring Mission that controlled the blockade, and it was headed by a Swedish general, Bo Pellnas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do know at the railway bridge, but there were breakthroughs of the blockade upstream along the River Sava, upstream from Raca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't the bridge that was used to break through the blockade but the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know that oil was transported in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Then you know more than I do. Tell me, and this agreement of yours to form a Serbian Democratic Party of Serbian Lands, did it imply joining forces for the elections in Serbia so that I would be replaced by you and the Serbian Democratic Party of Republika Srpska? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that the SDS of Krajina should be absorbed within his party so that he should appear at the elections in Serbian Krajina and to have political control over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement that I heard and remember well, didn't you say that the SDS of Serbian Lands was going to go participate at the elections in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS of Krajina did not join that SDS of Serbian lands. That party was an opposing party to the SDS of Krajina at the elections in Krajina at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it take part as an opposition party in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS of Krajina, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the SDS of Serbian lands, did it participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go on, then. Is it true that while the Assembly was in session, Grahovo fell, as had happened to Glamoc, and then the Assembly of RSK proclaimed a state of war and instructed your government to be permanently in session in Knin? On the 27th of July, 1995, a new government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was formed headed by you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And on that same day, we were informed that the Croatian army, the HVO, and other formations had captured Bosansko Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was a decision then taken that you should sit permanently in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The decision was taken for the government to sit permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Since such a decision was taken for the government to sit continuously and that a conflict was clearly in the offing, how did it happen that you fled from Knin together with your wife, children, and mother-in-law two days prior to the Croatian offensive? Were you informed about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not true I fled from Knin. In the last week of July, Yasushi Akashi was in Knin, the head of the UN mission for the former Yugoslavia, and during talks that he had with representatives of the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, he informed me that the American Ambassador Peter Galbraith, who I had met earlier, wanted to continue discussions with me about the so-called Z-4 plan, that is, the political status of the Serbian Krajina or, rather, the status of the territory that constituted the Serbian Krajina at the time. I accepted the invitation and a meeting was scheduled through Juri Mijakotnik, the head of the UN mission in Sector South, and it was scheduled for a Wednesday - I have to think over the date - in the American embassy in Belgrade, and that was the reason why I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was in Zagreb and you were in Knin. Why didn't you talk in Knin, but rather both of you had to go to Belgrade to meet there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first proposal was that we should talk on a boat, on a ship, and that I should be transported by helicopter via Split to that ship. And I said that that wasn't convenient, that it was safer for me to have the meeting in Belgrade. Martic and the others proposed that it should be in the office of the Krajina -- in the Krajina offices in Belgrade, but through Mijakotnik, I proposed a meeting in the American embassy in Belgrade as it was safer and more accessible for me, and he accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not comply with the decision of the Assembly for the government to be continuously in session in Knin but you left Knin on the 2nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the decision of the government, not the Assembly. The Assembly doesn't decide how the government will sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, fine. But the decision was for it to sit permanently because of the danger. How could you leave Knin, and how did you remember taking your wife, children, and mother-in-law with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left in the capacity of Prime Minister for -- to negotiate with international mediators regarding the political status of Krajina and preventing Krajina being captured by force of arms and for a political solution to be found for Krajina. That was the reason. Each member of the government had his assignments. And my priority at that point in time was to find a political settlement for Krajina and to accept the Z-4 plan which I supported as Foreign Minister during two conversations I had with Galbraith but whom I had informed previously about the political relationships and the balance of forces in Krajina and around Krajina with regard to the acceptance of that plan. When I became Prime Minister, my political authority increased, and as the Prime Minister, I was able to accept that document, and that was the reason why I gladly and immediately agreed to that talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you haven't answered why you needed to take your whole family to the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family did not attend the negotiations. They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But why did you take them to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were they then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother-in-law was very seriously ill. She was suffering from cancer, and she needed treatment, and she went for treatment several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But where were they physically? Would you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
