utterances.text: They were not with me. They did not -- they were not involved in politics. They have nothing to do with my political decisions and my political activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: M. Babic, what is being put is that you fled with your family. Now, you say that you left because you were attending, wanting to go to a meeting and wanting to attend talks. Now, what you are being asked about is if it's right that you were going to the political talks, why was it necessary for your family to go? Your answer is that your mother-in-law needed treatment. Now, can you just explain, if it's the case, why was it necessary then for the rest of your family to go too? Can we just hear your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mother-in-law didn't go with me. She was accompanied by my wife. There was a holiday, a school holiday. The children were on holiday, and I wanted them to be safe. It was a highly unsafe situation. I didn't have any special protection at the time, and there was fighting around Knin. My mother-in-law died one month or two months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there no dispute, then, that you left Knin together with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went on my -- to do my own business, and they went to take care of their own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't claim that you took your mother-in-law, wife, and children for talks with Galbraith. I just asked you whether you went together with them from Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the same day, yes. We didn't use the same transport, nor the same route, nor on the same business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never assumed that your wife and children took part in the negotiations. I just said that together with them you left Knin, two days prior to the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered the matter. He's given his explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With great effort. I wouldn't ask you, if you were a witness, about your family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not your family that is in question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's not an improper question. It's relevant. You see, the issue is -- the accused is putting that you fled and you took your family with you. He's entitled to put that. You've given your explanation. Now, Mr. Milosevic, unless you've got some new point to make on this, we should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain to me now: You said here, in private session, that you had agreed with Galbraith, or rather, that you accepted, in talks with Galbraith, the plan for a settlement that was offered to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the elements I agreed with in the capacity of Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. From what has been shown to us here, on that day there was a meeting in Geneva, chaired by Thorwald Stoltenberg, and you sent some ministers there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Minister of Foreign Affairs went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Martic sent three negotiators. So the government sent one and the president of the Republic sent three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Answer this very specific question for me, please: If you say that you accepted the proposals given to you by Galbraith, why didn't you inform your negotiators in Geneva that you had accepted it, so that they might tell their collocutor in Geneva, that is, the Croatian side, about it? Why didn't you inform them of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I talked to Milivoje Vojnovic, the Foreign Minister of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, who was a member of the delegation, and I talked to Milo Novakovic, who was also a member of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you informed them that you had accepted, and they didn't say so over there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what I had accepted, and my suggestion was that they accept all the proposals of the international mediators, and they did accept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. If they accepted, as you are saying, the proposals of the international mediators, why does it emerge from the note written by the British ambassador, as far as I could see, a note to the governments of participating countries, that Stoltenberg had told them from Geneva that they were not informed about anything? Does that mean that they informed their collocutor or they didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know what I said here. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I haven't finished my answer. I was told by people who listened to Pasalic, who was a member of the Croatian delegation, that he said that the Serbs were buying time. So according to my direct knowledge, the Croatian delegation was informed, and as far as I know, and this was what Ambassador Galbraith told me, and he had discussed my statement with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that the Croatian side knew that you had accepted the proposals. That means that the American side knew that you had accepted the proposals. But nevertheless, the very next day an offensive was launched by the Croatian army, encouraged by those same Americans whose propositions you had accepted, and an offensive of the army which had been informed about your acceptance launched the offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had informed the ambassador that those proposals can be implemented only if you agree with them. I was informed -- or rather, the doubts were expressed of the international mediators as to Martic's agreement with it, and also I was told that they had information - and I was told this by an official of the French embassy - that you were not supporting this, and this was on the day the Croatian offensive and the bombing of Knin by the Croatian army started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say here that you called me and informed me that you had agreed, and that I had said, "Fine, calmly," or "peacefully"? Those were your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I quoted you as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear -- but I also saw, on the videotape of your interview, explaining a conversation with me, you said that you had asked me about the Z-4 plan and that I had said that the plan was a good one. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, only that Slunj needs to be divided vertically, though Slunj should have been part of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why you said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that either, but that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I did say that the plan was good, didn't I? Then why are you accusing Martic that he said the plan should not be taken into consideration when you yourself say that Martic said that the plan cannot be reviewed until the mandate of the UN is extended? Are these two different things or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not accusing Martic. I'm just conveying his words, that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said that the plan should not be even taken into consideration until the Vance Plan was implemented. And at that point in time, there was a new idea, a new concept, the UNCRO mandate of the peace forces, not the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan was no longer a plan of the international community. That plan was something that you did not comply with. You did not implement it. You did not allow demilitarisation. And in 1995, you said that the proposal for a political settlement should not be even considered until the plan that you obstructed is implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And isn't it true that Boro Mikelic said that it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He went to the next-door office and talked to him, or telephoned - I don't know - but he sat there and kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how do you link this up, then, with your conversation with me where I said that the plan was a good one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the facts. I'm stating the facts. You were deceiving me. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I was deceiving you, and behind your back I told Martic not to even consider the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what Martic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. That's what Martic said, and I told you something else. So the important thing is what Martic told you that I had said and not what I had told you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The important thing is what you did and how you behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you yourself explained that Martic had said to the representatives of the international community: We're not going to consider it until the mandate of the United Nations is revived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance Plan. The Vance Plan was extended, renewed, in a different way, and it was UNCRO later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You never mentioned Vance's plan. Vance's plan was already four years old at the time. So whether it was UNPROFOR or UNCRO, there's no difference there. It was a mandate given to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The United Nations renewed their mandate in a different way and UNCRO was formed later on, so until the plan -- Vance's plan was realised; at least, that's what you had said. And the plan was no longer in the offing among the international community. It was not implemented because you obstructed its implementation. And you prevented the demilitarisation of Krajina and remilitarised it again, and this was in opposition to the plan. And all this happened in the second half of 1992, in 1993, in 1994, and in 1995 as well. And even when you spoke to me, when you said that the plan, the Z-4 plan, was a good one, when you said that to me, you also said, in the same breath, that the logistics of Serbia was with us in the fight against Croatia. So those were your words as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. C-061, let's not make these fabrications and constructions, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You put Milo Brksic [phoen] in command of the operations in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't announced a tape, and I don't want to abuse the time or use up my time in this way, but I shall be showing you an excerpt of what you yourself said, a tape of that, and then we'll be able to see what it was that I did and just how many untruths there were in your statements and testimony itself. But let's not discuss that point now. From what you said here during your examination-in-chief, it would appear that Galbraith told you that a Croatian offensive was in the offing, that it would follow. Is that right, Mr. C-061?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in those very words, but that was the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. That was the sense of it. If we did not react, that Croatia would. But did you inform anybody of this? Because you were the only man who knew about this Croatian offensive. So did you inform anybody about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a conversation in the evening, between 8.00 and 10.00, one or two hours. And the next day I made a statement, and I talked to you, I talked to Vlatkovic -- Vlatko Jovanovic, and I said what I had agreed with Galbraith. I asked for your support in the matter. I made my statement, and the negotiations took place in Geneva, and the next day the Croatian offensive started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you inform anybody? Why didn't you tell anybody that a Croatian offensive was in the offing, if Galbraith had indeed told you, as you yourself say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said something along those lines, that Croatia would opt for a military settlement. He didn't say the Croatian offensive would begin the next day. He said that we would fare the same as Western Slavonia. So it was by way of a comment on his part. He didn't actually announce a Croatian offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't become conscious of the fact that he knew something about a Croatian offensive of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the intermediary in the talks between me and Tudjman, or rather, as I understood it, he proposed the American concept that Krajina -- according to which Krajina, or rather, its part, which was called SAO Krajina, be given political and territorial autonomy in Croatia. That was the Z-4 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was their proposal. That was their proposal. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. What I'm asking you is this: Are you saying that it wasn't clear to you at that time, that he did not inform you that there would be a Croatian offensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that Croatia would settle the issue militarily and that it would be detrimental to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anybody about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I talked about that and I took steps to prevent it. I accepted his views and stands. I asked your support. I called upon the delegation in Geneva to accept it. So as far as I remember, those were the political moves I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave your political moves aside, and answer my question directly. Did you inform anybody whatsoever that Galbraith told you that there would be a Croatian offensive to follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that we would fare badly unless we agreed and accepted, so I urged that we did, in fact, accept. He didn't say that there would actually be a Croatian offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't know that there would be a Croatian offensive; is that what you're saying? Let's clear up one point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had no idea that there would be one so fast, especially as we had made the statement. I had made a public statement saying that I accepted and that the delegation in Geneva accepted the proposals made by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's put all the pieces of this puzzle together, and the facts. You accepted the proposals, the Geneva delegation accepted the proposals, the Croatian side was informed that the agreement had been accepted, the American side and the other sides were also informed, because they had talks with you, and nonetheless an offensive did follow. Are those the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, is it also true that once the offensive was launched in the -- early in the morning the next day, you personally, from the bureau of the government in Krajina in Belgrade, sent faxes to Dvor na Uni and Kostajnica to tell people to withdraw? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Milivoje Vojnovic sent some form of correspondence along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about Vojnovic. I don't even know what your representative's name was in Belgrade. What I'm asking you is about you personally. Did you send faxes to Kostajnica and Dvor na Uni that people were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just see if we could move back into open session at this point. Let me just check. Well, quite simply, I'd like to link all this up, what you're saying now with what was presented here as being intercepts; that in 1991, on the 11th of December, 1991, a conversation between myself and Karadzic - and it is page 0212900 - that you intentionally tried to give Tudjman an alibi for this entire situation, or, for example, the conversation on the 23rd of November. I don't even want to quote what I said on that occasion. But that you were leading up to the fact that your people would be slaughtered, that Tudjman would step on you, and I said that you were a rascal. So those are your exhibits, exhibits that were put forward here. Was I right, then, in 1991, Mr. C-061? Wasn't I right when I qualified you in that way, in view of what you've just recounted to us all here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were not right. You were in favour of the Vance plan and demilitarisation. But you did not fulfil Vance's plan, which you advocated, and you hold me responsible. It is a fact that I was against the plan and asked that it be modified. But it is a fact that you came out in favour of the plan and forced the Krajina Assembly to adopt the plan, and then you violated the plan. You didn't respect it. Those are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that precisely in conformity with that plan, that the JNA withdrew from the area of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA did withdraw, but the weapons remained. And a portion of the officers stayed on in the TO. General Torbica became the commander of the Territorial Defence, the structure of the Territorial Defence stayed on, and in 1993 everything was -- became a function of the general situation, as an army, as the Serb army of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The last reference is to Exhibit 353, tab 45. Yes. There seems to be some doubt whether it's 44 or 45. One of the two. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Anything more in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think that we need remain in private session for what I'm getting to, Mr. May, but we'll see, and you can assess for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go on in private session and just see what happens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think we need continue in private session, because I'm moving on to another area which is just linked to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go, then, into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the light of everything that we have heard thus far, Mr. C-061, tell me this: In addition to the fact that you're testifying against me, are you also a suspect of this institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not testifying against you; I am testifying to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These matters were discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Private session. 24 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, M. Babic, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've put something to the witness. He should have a chance to answer it. Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, he claimed that I was testifying against him. I am testifying about the truth; neither for nor against, but the truth as I know it. And what was the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question was: Are you also a suspect, a suspect of the Tribunal? And am I right if I say that you are a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told, when I had the first contacts with the investigators and the Prosecution of this Tribunal, that I was also a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why were you a suspect? Did they explain to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. According to a paragraph in the indictment that charges you, one of the charges against you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you are not an accused; right? You have not been accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have the assertions of the representative of the Prosecution here, and I think it is up to the OTP to answer that question, once again, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you say you regret and are sorry and that you have responsibility, and as you claim that something happened which did not happen, because that is what the Prosecutor expects of you, and you say that you didn't make a deal of any kind, do you know why you haven't been arrested? Why haven't they arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, Mr. C-061. And tell me this. Let's be more precise. Let me put my second question again. Did you first express your desire to testify before this Tribunal, or were you first a suspect and then came by the idea that through your testimony you could accuse me for the crimes that were committed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me be quite precise. It was suggested, it was proposed, that I be a witness in another investigation, at the end of the year 2000, or 2001. However, I decided that I would like, when the International Tribunal has its branch in Belgrade, or rather, when the authorities of Yugoslavia accept the International Tribunal on its territory -- they asked me to go to Banja Luka to testify, in fact. I couldn't go to Banja Luka. I had no passport of any kind, Yugoslav or otherwise, and I was afraid of going there because I didn't think I would be allowed to return to Belgrade. I lived in Belgrade. So that's the first point. The second point is that when I heard, through the media, my name mentioned in the indictment of the Tribunal against Slobodan Milosevic, I felt the need and duty, first of all for my own personal reasons, to make -- to set up contact -- to establish contact with the Tribunal and to tell the representatives of the OTP everything that I know about the events that came to pass, including my own participation in them, and that was the reason why I asked for these contacts with the Tribunal. We established contact and our talks began. They were tape-recorded, and you have them here, and you are now presenting part of those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From this very unwieldy explanation, am I able to draw the conclusion that when you made this statement, you in fact knew that you were one of the suspects; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time at the beginning of each interview I was told what my status was and what my rights were. I was read my rights. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as this also is something we ought to discuss in private session to avoid any reactions, we can continue in private session, but tell me, please, in the statement that you gave to the investigators, you say that your letter dated the 12th of January - I don't want to quote it because it was the topic of a long debate between you yourself and the investigators and representatives of the opposite side - that your letter -- that you in fact did not write this letter. Is that right? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed that letter, but the letter was compiled by Borivoj Rasuo on the 12th of January, 1992, if that's what you mean, if that's what you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's tab 79, with the two letters from January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Rasuo wrote it; is that right? Do you mean to say that you weren't capable of answering, of writing an answer, or did you in fact agree with me and Rasuo did not, and then you accepted his text because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you didn't have your own position and stand, or what other point or explanation would be that somebody made a draft for your own letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have my stand and stance, but he was a better letter writer, he was better at rhetoric, and he advised me that they should be the reasons why we should proceed in that way, and I agreed with him. I agreed with his opinion, because I believed him. He was a politicologist, a political scientist, and I was a dentist. But I did have my political stance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. But did he express your views to the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my basic positions, yes, he did express them, and I already said that he embellished them, to use a literary term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that this man, Rasuo, after the meeting held in Belgrade on the 9th of March, went to the Democratic Party which was then represented by Micunovic, Kostajnica, Djindjic? Is that right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I did know that the information two years ago was that he was a councillor and that's how he introduced himself in the Democratic Party whose president was and is Zoran Djindjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the present Prime Minister of the puppet regime in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I don't think he was in Democratic Party, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was he your main advisor for political issues throughout that time and a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He became a friend of mine and my political advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I gathered from a part of your answer on the tape that this letter was written in a climate and atmosphere that I had created, as if Rasuo wanted to meet me halfway by sending that letter with the gross criticisms at my expense. Isn't that right? What was the purpose of that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was thinking back in retrospect. I was think about the events in retrospect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Tell me, please, is it true that the purpose of your letter was for you to compromise as much as you possibly could what I was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to compromise that but to express my political views and to oppose the concept that you were imposing on the people of Krajina or, rather, which you had accepted without prior agreement of the people or the representatives of the authorities in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that that same Rasuo, being aware of the time of the Milosevic-Seselj conflict, initiated the signing of a coalition agreement between you and Seselj in Belgrade in February 1994? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that on the basis of that coalition agreement which you and Seselj signed, the Serbian Radical Party, in March 1994, got the place, the position of the president of the Assembly of RSK, and his name was Branko Vojnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that then Milan Martic, as president of the RSK, did not wish to nominate you as the Prime Minister but, rather, Borislav Mikelic, whereby the coalition agreement was called in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martic had the obligation to propose someone from the majority party in the Assembly, and it was noted that the proposal of the majority in the Assembly was that I should be the one. Martic did not respect that, and he forced Borislav Mikelic, he imposed Borislav Mikelic. And I heard later from him that he was your choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you heard from him is not important. What is important is that he wouldn't agree to your coalition agreement with Seselj for the government to be handed over to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't respect the constitution of RSK for the position of Prime Minister to be held by a representative of the majority in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then you insisted that Rasuo be Minister of Information in Mikelic's government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first wanted it to be Lazar Macura, the Information Minister, but Martic and Boro Mikelic didn't agree with that, or, rather, Martic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you accepted Rasuo, who was even worse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agreed with that, as did Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you then become Minister of Foreign Affairs in that government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at the same time, you had control of -- shall I call it the majority in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The SDS of which I was the president did not have a majority in parliament, nor did it have a majority of the ministerial posts in the government. That was how the political forces were distributed in the Assembly and in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that this Rasuo of yours, a member of your party, your friend, your political advisor, all talks and negotiations with Croatia were obstructed by him and throughout the time published articles against me? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rasuo was against the negotiations of the government and my participation in negotiations with Croatia on an economic agreement, and that was the reason why he left the government and broke off all political and friendly relations with me and became not only in the opposition but a fierce critic of me and my policies. What he said about you in those days, I cannot remember clearly. I can't -- I am unable to comment on that. I don't know what exactly you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at least vaguely how many base attacks he launched against me? I assume following your instructions, or maybe they were not on your instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From October 1994, we broke off political contacts, and he became my political opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did he become your political opponent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of the autumn of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I have information here that he was replaced from the position of minister in December 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the opposition started immediately after we started economic talks with Croatia. He resigned - he wasn't dismissed - because he didn't agree with the policies of the government and with my own personal policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you saying that Jovica Stanisic allegedly approved that he should be minister? Of course he couldn't approve or disapprove of that because that was not his job, but you do know that he had very bad relations with Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April 1994 when the talks were conducted on the composition of a new government of the RSK, these talks were conducted in Martic's residence in Belgrade behind the Zvezda stadium, Jovica Stanisic, Brana Crncevic, and some others were present at those talks, and I've already referred to the situation when I proposed Lazar Macura. Martic opposed this. Then I said, "Let it be Borivoj Rasuo." Then Martic said, "He's even worse." And then Jovica Stanisic nodded in approval, saying it's okay, and then Martic said it was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't go into the nodding of heads, but tell me, please, your political advisor, your friend, your minister, your alterego, if I can put it that way, you yourself said that he obstructed all talks with Croatia while you are talking about some sort of gradual integration in those interviews that we viewed on tape. What kind of gradual integration of Krajina in Croatia and the settlement of the position of Serbs in Croatia can we talk about? And you're saying that I torpedoed your peace attempts and that you favoured a peaceful settlement whereas I wanted war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer to your first question is that Borivoj Rasuo had political influence over me in January 1992. Borivoj Rasuo had no political influence over me in the autumn 1994 and 1995 when the negotiations started. And you torpedoed the Z-4 plan because you prompted Martic not to take it into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martic said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So you're testifying about what Martic said. That is how you behaved. Tell me, was a session of the Assembly held in Glina on the 9th of February, one that you didn't wish to attend and that, after the debate, the Vance Plan was adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that that was a part of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina convened by Mile Paspalj, that that Assembly accepted the Vance Plan in the way I've already described, with the participation of General Adzic, other generals and their escorts, Kostic, Jugoslav -- Branko Kostic, Jugoslav Kostic, Kostic, members of the government of Serbia, and a very large delegation from Serbia. I've already described how that Assembly accepted the plan, that is, the way you had posed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you said that the three-day meeting held with the Presidency of Yugoslavia was something you fled from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the simplest explanation is that I didn't want to go back and be exposed to continued torture. I had already explained my position, and there was no further reason for me to be tormented at that session any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say after that that allegedly Jovica Stanisic told you that I had given him the assignment to arrest you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Jovica Stanisic was in Knin, he commented those events from the past, and he said I could have behaved in such a way that the Assembly accept the plan, and I could have agreed with the decision of the Assembly, and in that way I would have politically survived. And then his comment was that President Milosevic had told him to arrest me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand that. In what did I tell him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When there was this discussion or, rather, attempt to impose the Vance Plan during a three-day session of the Presidency in Belgrade, January, February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any explanation, if it is true that I told him that and if your assumption is true that he was a loyal associate of mine, that he would have told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that his assessment was -- I don't know whether he shared that assessment of his with you or not, that this would have inflicted political damage to you. Because I asked him, "Well, why didn't you arrest me?" Because then I would have become a visible political victim. Until then, I was an invisible political victim of your dictatorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were you an invisible political victim, when I wrote you a letter publicly, in public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did that for three months. In the -- in the same way, accept fully and unconditionally. So no discussion about modifications, no discussion about anything. I just had to accept something that you had already approved. That was your position from November 1991, December. Then the letter came in January, and then February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So you said that we saw each other for the first time sometime in October 1990, when you were talking about participating in the elections, and then you sort of followed some sort of policies of mine from October 1990 until November 1991, when we clashed. Is that right? So how shall I call it? This link of yours with my policies, as you would have it, lasted for some 11 months, though when you came to ask about elections, it had nothing to do with my policies because that wasn't any real meeting. So what are we going to do now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My direct contacts in connection with your policies went on from the 11th of August, 1990. I didn't see you in person, but we contacted through Slobodan Vucetic, and you sent the message through Borisav Jovic that you would support all our political struggle, that the JNA would be the guarantor of our political struggle, which meant also the calling of the referendum. That was the direct message.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's make ourselves quite clear here. You are sending a message to me via Vucetic that you want to talk to me, and I am on a summer holiday, and you're given the answer that you can talk to Jovic because your questions can be addressed, if you have any complaints, at the level of Yugoslavia and not at the level of Serbia, and that's all that you got as an answer. You were given an answer regarding the technical requests for being received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Vucetic said that you were over there, Kadijevic, and Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And another 3.000 or 4.000 guests.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about the other guests. And that you were there together and that we should send an official request to be received to Jovic, that he would hear us out and that he would tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. That you should call him seems to me logical. That is the proper institution because that is the federal Presidency. So they adopted the Vance Plan. Is it true that the vast majority of citizens, in spite of the fact that you did not accept the plan, was unconditionally in favour of peace, and that leaflets and the posters for the referendums posted by your men in Knin only confused the people? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is correct is that 5.000 citizens, a large number of the citizens of Knin, attended a rally and supported me at the end of the session in Belgrade. This was at the beginning of February. And for us to really have a clear picture of what the citizens were in favour of and what they were not in favour of, we wanted to call a referendum for the citizens to state clearly whether they were for the Vance Plan unconditionally or with the modification of the government of the RSK. As for leaflets and posters, I heard that the commander of the brigade in Gradacac which had two names, 1st Partisan Brigade and 1st TO Brigade, prohibited public information to be given to citizens about these things. So this didn't happen because there was a lack of political strength and power for this to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Milosevic, for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, Mr. May, has to do with the report of the command of the 9th Corps dated the 20th of February, 1992, which the other side has tendered. It is SAO34420, and I will quote from it as you've already had it in your hands, and I would like to hear comments. I will only quote from that report addressed to the commander of the 2nd Army, the commander of the 2nd Military District. "The very concept of Babic's and Vance's conditions in the leaflet seem to most voters unclear, and at first glance, they immediately reject the variant under B and to support the first variant, the first option, which is, of course, yours. On the other hand, all the citizens of Krajina are unconditionally in favour of peace and the arrival of the Blue Helmets so that the referendum posters are only causing confusion so that the people don't know whom to trust any longer. "In Glina, on the 16th of February, an Assembly of the RSK was held, chaired by Mile Paspalj, and it adopted a decision on relieving Babic from the position of president of the republic and also adopting a no-confidence towards the whole government." And it also says this session that you claim was held under pressure, the session was attended by 85 deputies, of which 74 favoured the decisions, 8 were against, and 3 deputies refrained from voting, abstained. "Already at 1855, on Serbian Radio Knin, a telephone conversation was held with Milan Babic in which he said that the session in Glina was unlawful and that it was held upon instructions from Belgrade." That is one extract. This is quite a long report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't think we can embark on this at the moment. Is there anything you want to ask about that particular Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extract which the witness can deal with quickly or we'll leave the matter until next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, in the form of a question, I would like to ask him, which is one of the last quotations I wanted to read from this dispatch: "Milan Babic is endeavouring in every way to hold onto power in Krajina. When he saw he wouldn't have the support of the Assembly, he abruptly took a decision to form new municipalities in the villages in which he has loyal supporters. It is particularly conspicuous that some larger places in RSK, which were municipality centres, Udbina, Kistanje, are no longer treated as municipalities, though each of those places has more inhabitants than most of the newly formed municipalities taken together. And he's relying on a provision of the constitution, according to which the president is entitled to convene the Assembly." So not only did you not respect the decisions of the Assembly and all the recommendations that we gave, but you even sought at all cost to hold on to your political power in Krajina, especially with regard to this question on which our opinions clashed regarding the acceptance of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new municipalities that I initiated should be formed were later known as the pink zones, and they were parts of the RSK which had joined by referendums to one of the municipalities in Krajina and were not covered by the Vance Plan, and this was a political way of highlighting their position so that they would be given appropriate attention. And secondly, in regard to your statement that I wanted to remain in politics, I did. That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I have no more time for any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a reference to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not an exhibit. It is actually a document provided to Mr. Milosevic as Rule 68 material, and we have no translation. We have the Serbian version of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let it be exhibited, be given the next exhibit number, and we'll get it translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Defence Exhibit number is 59, D59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to adjourn now. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Open session. We're in closed session -- private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There will not now be time to conclude the evidence of the witness next listed before Christmas, and the decision has been taken that it would be inappropriate to have his evidence in two parts. He will therefore not now be taken until January at the earliest, and we will find and identify by Thursday morning at the latest other witnesses to fill the three plus one days remaining after the conclusion of this witness's evidence, by my calculation, on Friday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He's got about 14 hours outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. As to the next listed witness, there have been a number of difficulties. It is possible that, in respect of documentary provision, we will apply to the Chamber in the next few days for specific assistance, there being time between now and the date when the witness would be coming to Court for the Chamber to assist in dealing with that, a matter we regard as really non-compliance by the provider. Second point: The chronology that the Chamber required has been prepared and will be served tomorrow. It is at the moment sourced mainly to either the indictments or to the pre-trial brief, but of course the paragraphs in those documents provide further sourcing to raw material for most entries. The Chamber might have wanted to say something to the accused about how he might approach this document. We've sought to make the entries in it, entries in it that should be capable of agreement, and by indicating agreement to those entries, time can be saved, time which will thus be available for evidence in chief and in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll see the chronology when it comes. If there are matters which should not be subject of controversy, we'll invite the accused to agree them. You will let the accused have your list of witnesses, or your next witness, as early as you can, so you can prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will be tomorrow afternoon, or Thursday morning at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Very well. We'll adjourn now. M. Babic, would you be back, please, on Monday morning. Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of December, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.06 p.m.,
